questionStem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the office for a health maintenance examination. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Menopause occurred 1 year ago. She does not exercise. Her diet consists mainly of meat and potatoes with very few vegetables. She drinks one beer daily and four to five large cups of coffee daily. She had smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years, but quit 10 years ago. She works as a mechanic. She has no family history of cancer, but wishes to know what she can do to reduce her risk for breast cancer. The patient appears well. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (210 lb); BMI is 34 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely to reduce this patient’s risk for breast cancer?

choices.C: Exercising and reducing her caloric intake

correctExplanation: Exercising and reducing her caloric intake is the action most likely to reduce this patient’s risk for breast cancer. Breast cancer is the most common nondemartologic malignancy in women and commonly presents with a breast mass, skin or nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy. However, it may also be asymptomatic and diagnosed on screening mammography. Risk factors for breast cancer development include a family history of breast cancer, genetic mutations (eg, BRCA1 and BRCA2), early menarche, late menopause, and nulliparity. There are also several modifiable risk factors, including obesity, exogenous estrogen administration, alcohol and tobacco use, and lack of physical activity. Postmenopausal obesity, specifically, is associated with increased morbidity and mortality related to breast cancer. Treatment for breast cancer depends on its stage at diagnosis. In patients with early-stage disease, treatment consists of surgical removal of the tumor and axillary lymph nodes along with adjuvant systemic hormonal therapy, biologic therapy, or chemotherapy, which depends on the estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptor positivity of the cancer. Patients with advanced breast cancer are typically treated with life-prolonging, palliative systemic therapy only.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Abstinence from caffeine (Choice A) has not been associated with a decreased incidence of breast cancer. It is therefore not a modifiable risk factor for this patient.

Alcohol cessation (Choice B) may decrease this patient’s risk for breast cancer, as moderate alcohol use has been associated with an increased risk for breast cancer development in a dose-dependent fashion. However, although her risk is increased compared with a woman who abstains from alcohol use, her risk is more significantly increased due to obesity and lack of physical activity. Thus, the most appropriate next step in management is encouraging her to exercise and reduce her caloric intake in an attempt to lose weight.

Increasing her intake of soy (Choice D) has not been associated with a protective effect against the development of breast cancer. It would not be the most appropriate suggestion.

Raloxifene therapy (Choice E) is an estrogen modulator that is most commonly used in the treatment of osteoporosis, as well as in the prevention of postmenopausal breast cancer in patients at increased risk. However, this patient is not at increased risk for breast cancer and raloxifene would not be the most appropriate suggestion.

questionStem: A state-supported academic health and insurance system is contracted across a large state in the western United States to cover the aspects of care for patients of all ages and income levels, including the Medicaid and Medicare populations. The system's goal is to provide the highest quality of care in the most efficient manner to all patients equally and to support the productivity of the population in that state. The organization already has many skilled providers within every specialty, but they also wish to prioritize key areas for proactive improvement. Which of the following strategies is most likely to be effective in achieving this goal?

choices.A: Eliminate prior authorization requirements and expand drug formularies to include more prescription options
choices.B: Establish a mobile clinic to bring specialty services directly to underserved areas of the state
choices.C: Expand insurance access for specialty, advanced imaging, and surgical services
choices.E: Increase relative investment in primary care services

correctExplanation: Quality improvement is a framework that seeks to systematically improve and standardize the performance of a health care system. This vignette describes an intervention aimed at improving population health. Primary care has been shown to improve population health and decrease health disparities. The vast majority of medical care is delivered through primary care. As well, primary care commonly uses primary prevention strategies. Primary prevention strategies aim to prevent the effects of disease before the disease occurs (eg, diet, exercise to prevent diseases such as obesity and diabetes mellitus). Primary prevention strategies are effective across diverse subpopulations and are therefore an efficient means of increasing productivity by preventing disease across a population.
incorrectExplanation: Eliminate prior authorization requirements and expand drug formularies to include more prescription options (Choice A), establish a mobile clinic to bring specialty services directly to underserved areas of the state (Choice B), and expand telemedicine services (Choice D) would improve the health of certain subpopulations only. Expanding drug formularies and eliminating prior authorization requirements would affect only patients requiring specialized medications. Establishing a mobile clinic and expanding telehealth services would increase health outcomes for rural subpopulations or subpopulations without easy transportation, not the entire population. Expand insurance access for specialty, advanced imaging, and surgical services (Choice C) may increase health in a subpopulation with suboptimal insurance. However, it would not improve population health for the entire population. Additionally, specialty services provide tertiary prevention, which is defined by preventing complications of existing disease, rather than primary prevention. Primary prevention applies to more of the population than tertiary prevention, as tertiary prevention only applies to subpopulations that already have specific diseases.

questionStem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother for a well-child examination. The mother is concerned about nighttime bedwetting, reporting that although the patient has been toilet-trained for the past 2 years during the daytime, she has "never had a dry night." The patient has three siblings who the mother states were all dry through the night by age 5 years. The patient is otherwise healthy and vaccinations are up-to-date. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows no abnormalities. Fasting fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 82 mg/dL, and urinalysis is within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Enuresis is seen in approximately 15% of children and is defined as episodes of urinary incontinence in children age 5 years and older. Enuresis is divided into monosymptomatic and nonmonosymptomatic types. Monosymptomatic enuresis refers to nighttime bedwetting in children with no other lower urinary tract symptoms or history of bladder dysfunction and can be further classified as primary or secondary. Primary monosymptomatic enuresis refers to enuresis in children who have never been previously continent at night, while secondary monosymptomatic enuresis refers to enuresis that develops after a prior of at least 6 months of nighttime continence. Nocturnal enuresis occurs as a result of a combination of factors, including maturational delay, genetic factors, disturbed sleep, and detrusor overactivity. Evaluation of patients with nocturnal enuresis should include a thorough medical history and physical examination, as well as a urinalysis with the goal of determining whether the patient has an underlying pathologic cause to their bedwetting. History should focus on the presence of any lower urinary tract symptoms, frequency and trend of bedwetting episodes, stooling history, and social history. Urinalysis is done to screen for diabetic ketoacidosis, diabetes insipidus, and urinary tract infection. In almost all cases, monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis resolves spontaneously. For patients and/or parents who view enuresis as a problem (eg, interfering with social life) and wish to seek treatment, there are several options available. Primary management for enuresis involves treatment of coexisting conditions, patient and parent education, and motivational therapy, including reassurance. If the patient is still having bedwetting episodes after 3 to 6 months of initial therapy, desmopressin therapy or enuresis alarms may be considered.

questionStem: A 44-year-old man comes to the office because of a 5-year-history of a lump on his upper back. Four months ago, the lump became tender for 1 week when he had been exercising at the gym more often, but the tenderness resolved spontaneously. He says the lump has not changed in size and he has not noticed any skin changes. The patient is worried that the lump could be cancerous. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 24 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a 4-cm nontender, moderately firm, mobile mass between the right scapula and the spine. No other masses are palpated. Ultrasonography of the lump shows a well-defined mass with a homogeneous echotexture. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Lipomas represent benign tumors of mature adipocytes. Lipomas can develop at any age, and there is limited knowledge regarding the pathogenesis of these benign tumors. Clinically, lipomas present as solitary, painless, soft, mobile, subcutaneous tumors which range from a few centimeters to over 10 cm in diameter. Pathologic examination of lipomas shows mature adipocytes with small, uniform, eccentric nuclei. In cases of asymptomatic lipomas, clinical monitoring is appropriate. If patients seek definitive management secondary to symptoms or appearance, lipomas may be excised. Though they are generally considered benign and harmless, they have a rare chance of transforming into malignant neoplasms (liposarcoma).
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Excisional biopsy (Choice A) is used to diagnose cutaneous neoplasms, including melanoma. Excisional biopsies allow for removal of an entire suspicious lesion and permit a histologic diagnosis. While excisional biopsy may be used for suspicious lesions, the clinical examination and ultrasound findings in this case are consistent with lipoma which may be clinically monitored.

Fine-needle biopsy (Choice B) may be used to diagnose subcutaneous tumors, including breast masses or thyroid nodules. Fine-needle biopsies are often completed with ultrasound guidance to identify the region of interest, aspirate the tissue, and subsequently complete histologic examination. While fine-needle biopsy may be used for the diagnosis of subcutaneous nodules and tumors, it is not recommended in the management of benign lipomas.

questionStem: A previously healthy 19-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and fever. He has a muffled voice. His temperature is 39.4°C (103°F). Which of the following would warrant the need for surgical intervention?
correctExplanation: This patient likely has a peritonsillar abscess. A peritonsillar abscess is a localized accumulation of pus between the palatine tonsil and the pharyngeal muscles. It is a potentially life-threatening condition because of the risk for local swelling and compression of the airway. It is most common in adolescents, particularly those with a recent history of prior tonsillitis or pharyngitis. While the infection is often polymicrobial, gram-positive organisms such as Streptococcus or Staphylococcus species may predominate. Patients such as this one present with fever, sore throat, trismus, localized swelling and fluctuance overlying the tonsil, lateral deviation of the uvula, and may show signs of airway compromise, such as muffled voice or drooling. The diagnosis is clinical but may be supported by radiography. Treatment involves surgical intervention, such as needle aspiration or incision and drainage of the peritonsillar space, and antibiotic therapy to provide broad coverage of likely pathogens.
incorrectExplanation: Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy (Choice A), petechiae over the soft palate (Choice C), and pharyngeal exudates (Choice D) can all be present with bacterial or viral pharyngitis. While present in this patient, they do not indicate the presence of a peritonsillar abscess or other structural compressive lesion that would require surgical intervention. A peritonsillar abscess is indicated by the presence of the muffled voice, trismus, pharyngeal asymmetry, and uvular deviation. Tenderness of the trachea (Choice E) can be a symptom of tracheitis. Patients with tracheitis can present with stridor. Stridor refers to a high-pitched sound secondary to turbulent airflow from an underlying upper airway obstruction, often as a result of inflammation. It is not a symptom of pharyngitis or peritonsillar abscess and is not a condition that can easily be treated by surgical intervention. Rather, attention should be paid to airway management including the potential need for intubation and mechanical ventilation, and treatment of common pathogens including administration of antibiotics.

questionStem: A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of epigastric pain. The pain is most severe 1 hour after eating and is relieved by over-the-counter antacids. He has had no fever, nausea, or weight loss. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. He does not smoke and drinks one glass of wine with dinner daily. His pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 136/88 mm Hg. There is mild epigastric tenderness without rebound or guarding. The stool is brown, and test for occult blood is negative. His hemoglobin concentration is 13.8 g/dL. Liver function tests show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Peptic ulcer disease describes the presence of ulcers in the stomach or duodenum, which classically presents with worsening abdominal pain related to consumption (gastric) or lack of consumption (duodenal) of food. This patient has a chronic history of epigastric abdominal pain after eating that is relieved by antacids, making peptic ulcer disease likely. Gastric ulcers can be caused by prolonged or excess use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which leads to a reduction of prostaglandin secretion and decreased protection of the gastric mucosa. However, the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease is infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori, which accounts for nearly all duodenal ulcers. Thus, serologic testing for H. pylori with an antibody assay should be performed. Eradication therapy using a triple or quadruple combined therapy for H. pylori can eliminate the bacterium and permit healing of the peptic ulcer, generally with few complications if managed promptly.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Esophageal pH monitoring (Choice A) is a test used in the diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux disease when clinical findings and esophagogastroduodenoscopy are not adequate to confirm the diagnosis. Gastroesophageal reflux presents with chest discomfort, often in association with the consumption of a large meal or trigger food such as an acidic beverage, fatty food, coffee, chocolate, or tomato. It is often worse with supine positioning. This patient's symptoms arise 1 hour after consumption, and he has more epigastric rather than chest discomfort, making peptic ulcer disease more likely.

Measurement of serum amylase activity (Choice B) is used in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis, where serum amylase activity and lipase activity are commonly increased. Acute pancreatitis presents with severe epigastric abdominal pain that radiates to the back, along with nausea and emesis, often in a patient with a history of gallstones, alcohol use disorder, trauma, hypertriglyceridemia, or hypercalcemia. This patient has chronic, not acute, abdominal pain, no nausea or emesis, and no risk factors for acute pancreatitis, making this diagnosis unlikely.

Abdominal ultrasonography (Choice D) is the first-line diagnostic examination for the evaluation of potential cholelithiasis or cholecystitis. Cholelithiasis can present with postprandial epigastric or right upper quadrant pain. Acute cholecystitis occurs secondary to obstruction of the cystic duct from a gallstone, which results in subsequent inflammation of the gallbladder wall. It typically presents with fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and tenderness to palpation, often in a patient with a history of gallstones. This patient has no history of gallstones or signs of acute cholecystitis, and cholelithiasis would not be relieved with antacids, making these diagnoses unlikely.

questionStem: A previously healthy 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of palpitations and feeling hot, sweaty, and anxious. During the past 2 months, she has had a 3.2-kg (7-lb) weight loss despite a normal appetite. She has not had chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, dizziness, or nausea. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. Menses previously occurred at regular 30-day intervals, but she notes that during the past year she 'might have missed a few periods.' She does not smoke cigarettes. She drinks one glass of wine monthly. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 61 kg (135 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her pulse is 112/min and regular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Her serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is 0.1 μU/mL. Results of additional laboratory studies are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Fine-needle biopsy of the thyroid gland

correctExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism such as tachycardia, increased blood pressure, palpitations, anxiety, weight loss, and hot flashes. The patient was found to have low TSH concentration, indicating that the cause of her hyperthyroidism is likely a primary type (eg, Graves disease, hyperfunctioning thyroid nodule). On physical examination, the patient shows no signs or symptoms of a discrete thyroid mass. All patients with signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism as well as low TSH concentration should undergo thyroid ultrasonography along with testing for thyroid stimulating antibodies. Ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy can be performed at the same time, which is recommended for patients with risk factors for malignancy or for nodules with concerning ultrasound features. Subsequent workup and management is dependent on the results of the TSH concentration measurement, antibody detection, radioiodine uptake testing, characteristics of the nodule shown on ultrasound, and biopsy results. Of these options, ultrasonography is the best next step for this patient.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

Admission to the hospital (Choice A) is not necessary currently. The patient does not display any unstable vital signs or features within her history or examination that mandate hospitalization. Outpatient testing for hyperthyroidism can be performed for this patient given her stability. Should she develop signs of severe hyperthyroidism or thyroid storm, inpatient management would be warranted at that time.

Endometrial biopsy (Choice B) is not appropriate for the patient. This patient's inconsistent menstrual cycle can be attributed to her current hyperthyroidism, as is confirmed with the low TSH. Endometrial biopsy is not indicated at this time.

Fine-needle biopsy of the thyroid gland (Choice C) is not indicated at this time. The patient does not have a palpable thyroid nodule or any other concerning features that would warrant a biopsy. Thyroid ultrasonography is the best next step to evaluate for any nodules or other abnormalities.

131I therapy (Choice D) is not appropriate at this time. The patient requires further evaluation to determine the cause of her hyperthyroidism before any treatment is initiated. Radioiodine therapy is typically used for definitive treatment of hyperthyroidism, but it is not the next step in management.

questionStem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of difficulty sleeping and 'feeling worried and edgy most days.' She has been a patient for the past 10 years. She has no history of serious illness. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive. She works as an emergency room technician but is applying to nursing school next year. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she has an anxious mood and jittery affect. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) requires the presence of excessive worry about numerous aspects of daily life occurring on more days than not for at least 6 months, with consequent inability to control symptoms of anxiety and the presence of at least three other symptoms (including irritability, muscle tension, sleep problems, poor concentration, fatigue, restlessness). GAD may be associated with sympathetic hyperactivity, such as sweaty palms or panic attacks. The treatment depends on symptom severity. For mild GAD that does not affect daily function, as seen in this patient who still functions as an emergency room technician, office-based counseling is an appropriate initial step. This patient's anxiety should be monitored over the next few months. If office-based counseling is ineffective or if this patient presents with more severe dysfunction, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and/or cognitive-behavioral therapy should be started.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Alprazolam therapy (Choice A) is a benzodiazepine medication that can be used in refractory anxiety disorders in patients without a substance abuse history. Benzodiazepines do not play a role in initial treatment of GAD, as seen in this patient. Benzodiazepines are commonly used to manage anxiety as a transient side effect of SSRIs. As well, this patient's GAD is mild, so office-based counseling should be used before considering medications.

Diphenhydramine (Choice B) is a first-generation H1-receptor blocking agent that is commonly used for the treatment of allergies, insomnia, and motion sickness. It is sometimes used off-label as an as-needed medication for anxiety. However, it is not typically used as a first-line treatment for GAD. Also, this patient's GAD is mild, so office-based counseling should be used before medications.

Pregabalin therapy (Choice D) is an anticonvulsant medication that modulates calcium influx and thereby inhibits release of excitatory neurotransmitters, such as glutamate, norepinephrine, and dopamine. It is used in the treatment of seizures, generalized and social anxiety disorders, and neuropathic pain. However, it is not a first-line treatment for GAD. SSRIs should be used before considering treatment with pregabalin therapy. As well, this patient's GAD is mild, so office-based counseling should be used before any medications.

Valerian root supplementation (Choice E) is an herbal remedy with sedative and anxiolytic properties. However, in small trials, it has not been shown to be more effective than placebo. As such, it is not an evidence-based treatment for GAD. Also, this patient's GAD is mild, so office-based counseling should be used before medications.

questionStem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his parents are concerned that he is shorter than his classmates. He is at the 10th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Both parents are at the 75th percentile for height. His diet consists of cereal, milk, bread, and fried food. The patient's temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 75/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg. Examination shows sparse facial hair and sparse, straight, slightly pigmented hair at the base of a slightly enlarged penis. The skin is warm and moist. The testes are approximately 3 cm long and are descended into the scrotum bilaterally. X-rays show a bone age of 12 years (±4 months). Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient’s most likely diagnosis is constitutional growth delay, which is a normal variant of growth. Short stature has a variety of causes, such as constitutional growth delay, familial (ie, hereditary) short stature, chronic steroid use, endocrine abnormalities (eg, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency), cardiopulmonary disease, and genetic disorders (eg, Down syndrome, Turner syndrome). Familial short stature and constitutional growth delay are the most common causes of short stature. Constitutional growth delay is independent of parental stature, has a consistently decreased growth velocity, and a bone age younger than chronological age. Patients with constitutional growth delay may experience a delayed onset of puberty. These patients typically reach a normal adult height, with more rapid increases in height gain velocity as they progress through puberty.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Familial short stature (Choice B) typically presents in young patients whose parents are both of short stature with a normal growth velocity and bone age consistent with chronological age. These patients will remain of short stature into adulthood. This patient has parents with normal stature, making this answer less likely.

Hypothyroidism (Choice C) is commonly associated with short stature. However, patients are likely to report other symptoms of hypothyroidism, such as fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and dry skin. Also, this patient’s short stature began at an early age, which implies a chronic process. This patient does not have a history of a chronic illness, such as hypothyroidism.

Nutritional deficiency (Choice D) typically results in an abnormally low weight along with signs of malnutrition, such as dry skin and hair loss (because of decreased protein stores). This patient has a normal weight and lacks physical examination signs of malnutrition.

Normal development (Choice E) is associated with a bone age that is consistent with chronological age, which is not seen in this patient. Additionally, he is several standard deviations below the expected height for his age. This classifies him as having a growth delay, not just within the variations of normal development.

questionStem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient’s most likely diagnosis is constitutional growth delay, which is a normal variant of growth. Short stature has a variety of causes, such as constitutional growth delay, familial (ie, hereditary) short stature, chronic steroid use, endocrine abnormalities (eg, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency), cardiopulmonary disease, and genetic disorders (eg, Down syndrome, Turner syndrome). Familial short stature and constitutional growth delay are the most common causes of short stature. Constitutional growth delay is independent of parental stature, has a consistently decreased growth velocity, and a bone age younger than chronological age. Patients with constitutional growth delay may experience a delayed onset of puberty. These patients typically reach a normal adult height, with more rapid increases in height gain velocity as they progress through puberty.
incorrectExplanation:
Familial short stature (Choice B) typically presents in young patients whose parents are both of short stature with a normal growth velocity and bone age consistent with chronological age. These patients will remain of short stature into adulthood. This patient has parents with normal stature, making this answer less likely.

Hypothyroidism (Choice C) is commonly associated with short stature. However, patients are likely to report other symptoms of hypothyroidism, such as fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and dry skin. Also, this patient’s short stature began at an early age, which implies a chronic process. This patient does not have a history of a chronic illness, such as hypothyroidism.

Nutritional deficiency (Choice D) typically results in an abnormally low weight along with signs of malnutrition, such as dry skin and hair loss (because of decreased protein stores). This patient has a normal weight and lacks physical examination signs of malnutrition.

Normal development (Choice E) is associated with a bone age that is consistent with chronological age, which is not seen in this patient. Additionally, he is several standard deviations below the expected height for his age. This classifies him as having a growth delay, not just within the variations of normal development.

questionStem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
correctExplanation: This patient with dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and peripheral edema has a presentation consistent with ischemic cardiomyopathy, a kind of congestive heart failure (CHF). Physical examination classically shows peripheral edema, jugular venous distension (JVD), bibasilar rales, and an S3 or S4 heart sound. If taken, chest x-rays would likely show pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly, and laboratory studies would show an increased brain-natriuretic peptide concentration. Echocardiogram is the gold standard for diagnosis of CHF and may show either reduced ejection fraction in the case of systolic heart failure or preserved ejection fraction with diastolic heart failure. There are numerous causes of heart failure, including ischemic heart disease, hypertension, valvulopathy, pulmonary disease, infection, arrhythmias, and congenital causes. Treatment of CHF involves the management of underlying causes and associated condition, as well as appropriate pharmacotherapy to improve symptoms, preserve myocardial function, and reduce mortality. Initial recommended therapy generally includes a combination of five classes of medications: a beta-adrenergic antagonist, a renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitor, a diuretic, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. Treatment decisions are often nuanced and individualized depending on the degree of severity, presence of comorbidities, and potential drug interactions.
incorrectExplanation:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Choice A) classically presents with dyspnea, cough, and wheezing. While this patient has a diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and an extensive smoking history, his hypoxia is more likely a result of pulmonary edema in the setting of CHF. COPD in isolation generally causes right-sided heart failure, with peripheral edema, JVD, and pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary edema would not be explained in isolation by the hemodynamic consequences of COPD.

Community-acquired pneumonia (Choice B) classically presents with fever, malaise, and cough productive of sputum. This patient's orthopnea, pitting edema, and JVD are not consistent with an infectious process.

Metabolic syndrome (Choice D) is characterized by the constellation of insulin resistance, hypertension, high cholesterol, and abdominal obesity. Patients with metabolic syndrome, such as this patient, are at increased risk for cardiovascular disease, including ischemic cardiomyopathy. However, metabolic syndrome itself is not the direct cause of this patient's symptoms.

Pulmonary embolus (Choice E) is characterized by the sudden onset of dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxia. This patient's symptoms are more consistent with CHF.

questionStem: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of moderate back pain, fever, chills, and nausea. During this time, he also has had a burning sensation with urination and urinary urgency. He has a 3-year history of benign prostatic hyperplasia characterized by incomplete voiding and intermittent urges to void during the night. His medications are tamsulosin and aspirin. He appears ill. His temperature is 39.1°C (102.3°F). Percussion of the back elicits moderate discomfort. Abdominal examination shows diffuse tenderness to palpation but no rebound or guarding. Urine dipstick testing shows 2+ blood, positive nitrites, and positive leukocyte esterase. Results of urine culture are pending. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Pyelonephritis occurs because of the retrograde spread of a lower urinary tract infection. Urinary tract infections are more common in women due to the shorter urethra and favorable regional environment for bacterial growth and in patients with diabetes due to the presence of glycosuria. In men, benign prostatic hyperplasia and urinary outlet obstruction create increased risk for development of urinary tract infections. Upper urinary tract infections such as pyelonephritis more commonly present with systemic symptoms such as rigors, nausea, vomiting, myalgias, arthralgias, fatigue, high fevers, tachycardia, leukocytosis, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness on physical examination, such as in this patient with discomfort on percussion of the back. Urinalysis in pyelonephritis often shows greater than 10 leukocytes per high-power field and may show white blood cell casts. Bacteria are generally seen on microscopy, with gram-negative rods (especially Escherichia coli) being the most common pathogen. E. coli produces nitrites, detectable on urinalysis. Pyelonephritis is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

Citrobacter freundii (Choice A) is a cause of a variety of hospital-acquired infections such as pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and sepsis. questionStem: A 9-month-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. Developmental milestones are appropriate for age. She is at the 50th percentile for length and 60th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 137/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 86/42 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities other than mild conjunctival pallor. Her hematocrit is 29%, and mean corpuscular volume is 65 μm³. Which of the following questions would be most helpful to ask the patient's parents to determine the cause of this child's anemia?

choices.A: Did she have jaundice at birth?
choices.C: Has anyone in the family had their spleen removed?
choices.D: Has she passed any blood with her urine?

correctExplanation: Neonates and infants fed with only whole cow milk are at risk for developing iron deficiency anemia. Both breast milk and cow milk contain low concentrations of iron. The iron in breast milk has a high bioavailability while cow milk proteins impair iron absorption in human infants. In addition to poor absorption, cow milk is associated with increased occult enteric bleeding that contributes to iron loss during infancy. Most infants eventually tolerate cow milk later in life. Iron deficiency anemia early in life can lead to significant neurocognitive and psychomotor impairments that persist even after treatment.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and D.

"Did she have jaundice at birth?" (Choice A) is not the most helpful question as it does not help with identification of the underlying pathology. Newborn physiologic jaundice, also termed benign neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, occurs in nearly all newborns and is caused by the increased breakdown of red blood cells and resultant generation of bilirubin, the immature liver metabolism of bilirubin, and the increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. The presence of jaundice at birth would not help explain why this 9-month-old patient has microcytic anemia.

"Does she bruise easily?" (Choice B) is not the most helpful question. This would help to identify a history of bleeding issues from either platelet or factor dysfunction. Asking whether the patient bruises easily does not assist in determining the underlying cause for the anemia in absence of other evidence suggesting blood loss anemia, such as petechiae, bleeding gums, or dark or bloody stools. Because of this, it is more appropriate to ask about the patient’s diet to determine if that is a source of her deficiencies.

"Has anyone in the family had their spleen removed?" (Choice C) is not the most helpful question to ask. This question could be helpful in determining if a patient has a family history of hereditary spherocytosis. However, this condition would usually cause a normocytic anemia, not microcytic anemia as seen in this patient.

"Has she passed any blood with her urine?" (Choice D) is not the most helpful question to ask. Hematuria can have many causes in the pediatric population. Some examples are postinfectious nephritis, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, or IgA nephropathy. Given this patient has no recent history of illness or purpura, inquiring about diet would be most helpful at this time to rule out dietary deficiencies.

questionStem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the office because of a 1-day history of moderate left hip pain. He walks with a limp. Ten days ago, he had a mild cough and runny nose that resolved spontaneously. He has not sustained any trauma. He has no other history of serious illness and receives no medications. He appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, the left hip is in normal position. Palpation of the left hip joint produces no tenderness. Active and passive range of motion is limited by pain. Examination of all other joints shows no abnormalities. Results of laboratory studies are pending. Ultrasonography of the left hip joint shows a small amount of fluid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The most likely diagnosis in this otherwise healthy patient is transient synovitis of the hip. Transient synovitis is an inflammatory condition involving the synovial lining of weight-bearing joints, with the hip being commonly affected. It classically presents in children recovering from a viral infection with pain on weight-bearing, antalgic gait, refusal to ambulate, tenderness over the joint, and pain elicited with range of motion. Vital signs are generally within normal limits, as are laboratory studies with the exception of increased markers of inflammation such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein concentration. Antecedent viral infection has been reported in up to 30% of cases of transient synovitis. Diagnosis involves the exclusion of emergent or urgent conditions such as cellulitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and fracture. Treatment is supportive and involves rest plus nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications. If there is diagnostic uncertainty, arthrocentesis to exclude septic arthritis, along with imaging to assess for osteomyelitis or fracture, should be performed. In this case, the patient likely has transient synovitis, as ultrasonography shows a small amount of fluid and the patient has no history of trauma, in the setting of recent viral infection. The most appropriate next step is conservative management with ibuprofen therapy.
incorrectExplanation:
Ceftriaxone therapy (Choice A) or vancomycin therapy (Choice D) may be reasonable treatment options for cases of septic arthritis. Septic arthritis presents with a painful, erythematous, swollen joint with pain on passive range of motion. Joint aspiration classically discloses purulent synovial fluid with a leukocyte count greater than 50,000/mm3. Transient synovitis is the most likely diagnosis in this case of a 4-year-old with recent viral infection and lack of systemic symptoms.

MRI of the left hip (Choice C) may be used to evaluate further for hip pathology or osteomyelitis. If pelvic osteomyelitis is suspected, MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality to use. In this case, the patient does not have systemic symptoms but has a history of recent viral illness, making transient synovitis more likely. Conservative management with ibuprofen therapy would be the most appropriate next step in management.

X-ray of the left hip (Choice E) may be used to evaluate for fractures. In this case, the patient does not have a history of trauma, making fracture less likely. Because of his recent history of viral illness without current systemic symptoms, transient synovitis is the most likely diagnosis.

questionStem: A 16-year-old boy comes for an examination prior to participation in school sports. A painless mass is palpated in the scrotum; the mass decreases while supine and has a bag-of-worms sensation. The boy states that he did not notice it previously. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Varicoceles are caused by incompetence of the spermatic vein. They are more common in the left scrotum and may be asymptomatic or present with a dull, achy scrotal pain and heaviness. Physical examination will show a palpable, bag-of-worms–like mass that increases in size with standing and improves with lying down. The diagnosis is often clinical but can be aided by ultrasonography. Varicoceles are associated with infertility and testicular atrophy, and they may be managed symptomatically or treated with surgical correction.
incorrectExplanation: Epididymitis (Choice A), or infection of the epididymis, most commonly presents acutely with unilateral scrotal pain associated with a tender, swollen mass over the posterior aspect of the testis. It is most commonly caused by sexually transmitted infections in young men. Hydrocele (Choice B) is a collection of fluid within the tunica vaginalis. It presents as a painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates. Inguinal hernia (Choice C) may present as a scrotal mass, but it is usually reducible and may be associated with bowel sounds. Leydig cell tumor (Choice D) is a rare testicular tumor that may present with a testicular mass and hormonal symptoms such as gynecomastia. Teratoma of the testis (Choice E) is a germ cell tumor that presents as a painless testicular mass. Torsion of the testis (Choice F) presents acutely with severe scrotal pain and swelling, and it is a surgical emergency.

On physical examination, there is a soft, irregular mass in the left scrotum that increases in size with standing and decreases in size when the patient is supine. The mass does not transilluminate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Varicoceles are caused by incompetence of the spermatic vein and are more common in the left scrotum. They may be asymptomatic or present with a dull, achy scrotal pain and heaviness. Physical examination will show a palpable, bag-of-worms–like mass that increases in size with standing and improves with lying down. The diagnosis is often clinical, and they can be managed symptomatically or treated with surgical correction.

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the office because she is concerned about her risk for osteoporosis. Her 65-year-old sister recently sustained a hip fracture. One year ago, the patient sustained a fracture of her right wrist in a fall. She has no other history of serious illness. Menopause occurred 10 years ago. Her only medication is a daily multivitamin. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. She has a sedentary lifestyle. She is 152 cm (5 ft) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Her pulse is 64/min, and blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. The physician advises her to stop smoking, begin calcium supplementation, and begin a weight-bearing exercise program. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: DEXA scan at the age of 65 years

correctExplanation: Osteoporosis and osteopenia are metabolic bone diseases characterized by diffusely low bone density. The most common risk factors are age, smoking, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, and estrogen-depleting conditions. Such demineralization and low bone density is often asymptomatic but increases the risk for fractures, most commonly involving the hip, vertebrae, and distal radius. Diffuse osteopenia can be appreciated as radiolucent bones or fractures on x-rays. questionStem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of left ear pain for 2 days. She competes in long-distance open-water swimming events and trains in the ocean several hours daily. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the left ear shows erythema and edema of the auditory canal and a small amount of white discharge. Manipulation of the left pinna produces pain; the left tympanic membrane appears normal. After treating this patient for her acute condition, recommendation of which of the following is the most appropriate next step to prevent recurrence of this condition?

choices.B: Daily use of topical benzocaine in the ear canal
choices.C: Daily use of alcohol-acetic acid ear drops
choices.D: Daily use of carbamide peroxide ear drops
choices.E: Daily use of hydrocortisone ear drops

correctExplanation: Otitis externa, also known as 'swimmer's ear,' is related to inflammation of the external auditory canal. Otitis externa is associated with moisture that causes breakdown of cerumen and skin maceration. Additional risk factors for the development of otitis externa include aggressive ear cleaning, impediments like hearing aids or headphones, allergic contact dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis. Clinically, otitis externa patients may experience tenderness upon tragal pressure or pain with manipulation of the auricle. questionStem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 2-month history of progressive fatigue and lack of energy. During this time, she also has had a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss despite no changes in appetite or exercise. She has a 2-year history of frequent diarrhea. She has not had any abdominal pain but does have flatulence, which is worse when she runs. She is an avid runner and is preparing for her sixth marathon. Her medications are an oral contraceptive and over-the-counter loperamide as needed. She traveled to Peru 8 months ago. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 66 kg (145 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 60/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/64 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies are shown: Hemoglobin 11 g/dL, Hematocrit 33%, Mean corpuscular volume 72 μm3, Leukocyte count 6700/mm3, Serum ferritin 30 ng/mL. Results of a basic metabolic profile are within the reference ranges. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient’s diarrhea?

choices.B: Bacterial invasion of the bowel wall

correctExplanation: Villous atrophy in the small bowel is a characteristic finding of celiac disease. Celiac disease is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy that is mediated through immune intolerance of the protein gliadin, commonly found in wheat products. This results in inflammatory infiltration of the proximal small bowel, which leads to characteristic intraepithelial lymphocytosis, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia. Malabsorption of substances in the proximal small bowel ensues, which presents symptomatically as chronic diarrhea, weight loss, steatorrhea, and nutritional deficiencies. Iron deficiency is a common cause of anemia in patients with celiac disease. It commonly presents with microcytosis, with a mean corpuscular volume less than 80 μm3, such as in this patient, and an increased red blood cell distribution width indicating the release of premature erythrocytes, which are larger, from the bone marrow. The measurement of serum iron and ferritin is likely to show decreased concentrations, such as in this patient, which can confirm the diagnosis. Abnormal small bowel absorption in celiac disease results in abnormal serum D-xylose and fecal fat testing. D-xylose is absorbed passively in the proximal small bowel; reduced serum D-xylose indicates reduced small bowel mucosal surface area for absorption. The increased concentration of fecal fat indicates intestinal malabsorption of lipids, also seen in the presence of abnormal small bowel mucosa.

questionStem: An 86-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 4-day history of cough, diagnosed in the emergency department as pneumonia. The patient's medical record includes a signed and notarized living will dated 2 years ago that indicates his desire for no cardiopulmonary resuscitation or ventilation in the event of incapacitation, and administration of comfort measures only. Upon admission, the patient requests full resuscitation if his status should decline. The patient is oriented to person, place, and time. Initially, only oxygen via nasal cannula and antibiotics are administered, but overnight the patient's status worsens. In the morning, pulse oximetry on 40% oxygen administered via face mask shows an oxygen saturation of 85%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Adhere to the living will and provide morphine for comfort
choices.B: Ask the patient why his wishes changed
choices.C: Contact the hospital ethics committee to provide guidance
choices.D: Contact the patient's family to clarify his preferences

correctExplanation: Regardless of advance directives or prior code-status documentation, physicians need to assess all patients’ code status at each hospitalization, as the context of each hospitalization differs. The patient or the patient’s decision maker (eg, legal guardian or durable power of attorney) should be given the opportunity to update the patient’s code status. The patient expresses a preference to be full code, which signifies that life-prolonging care be administered while the patient is alive (eg, respiratory support, including with intubation, if lung function declines) and after the patient’s heart has stopped (eg, cardiopulmonary resuscitation). This preference supersedes his previously expressed preference for comfort care only, in which only medications that promote comfort are continued, while medications that solely prolong life are typically discontinued. Advance directives are legal documents that enable patients to dictate their preferences for end-of-life care ahead of time. Advance directives are especially important when patients become incapacitated and are no longer able to verbalize their wishes for care. However, capacitated patients can express wishes that supersede the preferences outlined in the advance directive, including preferences for code status. Since this patient is oriented and able to express a clear preference, the medical team should ventilate him, acting in accordance with his current wishes rather than his advance directive.
incorrectExplanation: Adhere to the living will and provide morphine for comfort (Choice A) violates the patient’s autonomy. He appears capacitated and expresses a preference to change his code status to full code, which supersedes the advance directive. As such, the medical team should administer life-prolonging care by ventilating the patient.

questionStem: During a routine health maintenance examination, a 15-year-old girl says that she has used marijuana with friends on four occasions. She is healthy and doing well in school. She requests that her parents not be told about the marijuana use. In addition to counseling her about the adverse effects of marijuana use, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention at this time?

choices.A: Referral to a psychologist for treatment of substance use disorder
choices.C: Scheduling a follow-up examination with the patient

correctExplanation: Parental consent is required for most medical care of minors (patients younger than age 18 years). Exceptions include medical care related to sexual activities (eg, sexually transmitted infection, contraception, pregnancy care), substance use, and life-threatening medical or psychiatric conditions. (Emancipated minors may make their own medical decisions.) For these sensitive or time-sensitive issues, patient confidentiality and autonomy are favored over other ethical principles. Respecting a patient’s wishes about disclosure of medical information can build therapeutic alliance and increase the chance that patients will continue to share sensitive information in the future. As such, the physician should respect this patient’s wishes to keep her marijuana use confidential. The physician should establish regular follow-up visits to monitor for adverse consequences of marijuana use (eg, cognitive impairment, psychosis) and the development of a use disorder.

questionStem: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of progressive pain and swelling of the left knee. She has pain with walking and at rest. There is no history of trauma. She has hypertension, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and asthma. Her current medications are insulin, a β-adrenergic blocking agent, and a daily inhaled corticosteroid. She is 158 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 136 kg (300 lb); BMI is 55 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100.1°F); other vital signs are within normal limits. The knee is tender, swollen, warm, and erythematous. There is severe pain with passive and active range of motion. Plain x-rays of the knee show periarticular osteopenia; the joint space is narrowed medially. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctExplanation: Septic arthritis classically presents with a painful, erythematous, swollen joint along with systemic signs and symptoms of illness such as fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia, and nausea. The affected joint discloses pain upon passive range of motion, swelling, and erythema on physical examination. Arthrocentesis is indicated for any case of monoarticular erythema and swelling to evaluate for septic arthritis, which characteristically reveals purulent synovial fluid with greater than 50,000 leukocytes/mm3. Serum tests may also show leukocytosis and increased inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein concentration and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Treatment involves urgent intravenous antibiotics with patients often requiring surgical irrigation of the joint. In this case, the most likely diagnosis is septic arthritis because of the patient’s presentation of increased temperature and erythematous joint with pain upon passive range of motion in the absence of reported trauma. questionStem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician with his wife because of a 6-month history of daytime drowsiness. His wife reports that he has had increased snoring, which is especially loud when he sleeps on his back, but he does not stop breathing for prolonged periods. The patient has a 15-year history of hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows an increased intensity of the pulmonic component of S2. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Headaches that occur in the morning, daytime sleepiness, and loud snoring are frequently reported by patients with untreated obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This patient is likely experiencing sleep-related hypoventilation as a result of OSA. Clinical features of untreated OSA include excessive daytime fatigue, falling asleep at inappropriate times, loud snoring, and a disrupted sleep-wake cycle. Risk factors include male sex, obesity, congenital or traumatic abnormalities of the oropharynx and upper airway, neuromuscular disorders, and use of sedating medications. Untreated OSA is associated with hypertension. Diagnosis is made via polysomnography testing. Management consists of lifestyle changes (eg, weight loss, dietary modifications, increased activity, changing sleep position), avoiding sedating medications and substances, and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) while sleeping. Second-line therapies include oral appliances, such as mandibular advancement devices for symptoms refractory to CPAP usage, and surgery for cases with obstructing lesions of the airway. Chronic, untreated OSA can result in pulmonary hypertension, which may manifest with heart murmurs or loud pulmonic heart sounds and eventual right-sided heart failure.
incorrectExplanation: ECG (Choice A) is not the most appropriate next step in management. While the patient has a history of hypertension and some cardiac risk factors, he has no symptoms that are indicative of cardiac origin. The loud pulmonic S2 is indicative of pulmonary hypertension likely caused by OSA. ECG would not be effective in diagnosing OSA in this patient, though it may show right-sided chamber hypertrophy. Echocardiography (Choice B) is not the most appropriate next step in management, though it may be indicated following polysomnography. This patient’s presentation raises suspicion for increased right-sided cardiac pressures, which would be diagnosed definitively with echocardiography, though he shows no other signs or symptoms at present. Patients with congestive heart failure have shortness of breath, edema, and potentially jugular venous distension. This patient does not display any of these symptoms or signs. Methylphenidate therapy (Choice C) or modafinil therapy (Choice D) are not commonly used for patients with daytime somnolence outside of narcolepsy or central apnea/injury. While methylphenidate or modafinil may be used to treat excessive daytime sleepiness, they do not address the underlying cause of OSA. Sleep positioning therapy (Choice F) is not commonly used for patients with daytime somnolence outside of narcolepsy or central apnea/injury.

questionStem: Results of HIV antibody and hepatitis C testing are negative. After reviewing the patient's results, a follow-up examination is scheduled for 3 days from today. In addition to measuring serum lithium concentration, which of the following tests is most appropriate to perform at this time?
correctExplanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism presents with hypercalcemia (which in turn presents with nephrolithiasis, chronic bone pain, abdominal discomfort, and psychiatric disturbances), hypophosphatemia, subperiosteal bone resorption, and end-stage kidney disease. Excessive production of parathyroid hormone results in increased serum calcium concentration from increased osteoclast activity, intestinal absorption, and renal tubular absorption. Serum phosphorus concentration is decreased secondary to increased excretion by the renal tubules. Patients with laboratory findings consistent with hyperparathyroidism, such as this patient with hypercalcemia, should undergo further evaluation with the measurement of serum parathyroid hormone concentration. Once confirmed, imaging studies may localize a parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma.
incorrectExplanation:
Bone density test (Choice A) is not the most appropriate next step for this patient. While this patient does meet screening criteria for osteoporosis given her age and sex, a DEXA scan to evaluate her bone health will not lend information toward why she has an increased calcium concentration. Because of this, serum parathyroid hormone concentration should be assessed first.

Renal ultrasonography (Choice B) is not necessary for this patient. This could lend information as to whether the patient has evidence of kidney disease, as a potential explanation for her increased creatinine concentration. However, measurement of serum parathyroid hormone concentration is more appropriate to assess the origin of her hypercalcemia, and additional testing could follow this if indicated.

Urinary calcium concentration (Choice D) is not necessary currently. Patients with chronic kidney disease commonly have increased excretion of calcium in the urine as they are unable to resorb and maintain serum concentrations over time. However, this would not provide further diagnostic information about the underlying cause of her condition.

X-ray of the spine (Choice E) is not appropriate at this time. Patients with multiple myeloma can have increased calcium, bone pain, anemia, and end-stage renal disease. X-ray of the spine can help assist in diagnosis and identification of lesions. However, it is more appropriate to assess this patient’s current parathyroid hormone concentration to identify the source of her hypercalcemia.

questionStem: An asymptomatic 42-year-old man with a 1-month history of essential hypertension comes for a follow-up examination. He has been moderately obese for 20 years and follows a high-calorie, high-fat diet. He drinks four to five cups of coffee daily. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He drinks one beer at dinner almost daily. He has a sedentary lifestyle. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m². His pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most effective method to decrease his blood pressure?
correctExplanation: Weight loss of 9 kg (20 lb) is the most effective intervention to decrease this patient's blood pressure. On average, for patients who are overweight or diagnosed with obesity, the loss of 0.45 kg (1 lb) of body weight correlates with a drop in mean blood pressure by around 1 mm Hg. Continued aerobic exercise at least several times per week will also help reduce this patient's blood pressure. Other interventions that are frequently helpful include dietary salt restriction, although many patients with essential hypertension will eventually require pharmacologic therapy to reduce their blood pressure below the current goal of 130/80 mm Hg. Particularly in young patients or those with ongoing hypertension despite the use of three medications including a diuretic, screening for causes of secondary hypertension should be considered.
incorrectExplanation:
Abstinence from alcohol (Choice A) is unlikely to have a meaningful effect on blood pressure in this patient who only drinks one beer daily. Male patients with hypertension who drink three or more drinks per day should be advised to reduce their intake to two or fewer drinks per day.

Abstinence from coffee (Choice B) is unlikely to affect this patient's blood pressure in a significant manner. The association between caffeine intake and long-term blood pressure is unclear, but regular intake of coffee is not thought to contribute to the development of primary hypertension. There may be a transient increase in the patient's blood pressure following consumption of caffeine; however, this will generally be brief and in temporal association with the duration of action of caffeine.

Smoking cessation (Choice C) is unlikely to affect this patient's blood pressure in the long term. Smoking has been shown to raise blood pressure transiently, while smoking the cigarette and in the minutes following, because of increased activation of the sympathetic nervous system. The effect on the blood pressure is transient with pressure returning to baseline within 10 to 15 minutes of finishing the cigarette. There has been no clear association between smoking and the development of chronic hypertension.

questionStem: An 88-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She has osteoporosis treated with alendronate. She also takes a vitamin D supplement. The patient underwent a DEXA scan within the past year; she demonstrated a stable bone density with a T-score of -2.3. She is still active in her community, but she lives alone. BMI is 21 kg/m². She has never smoked cigarettes and does not drink alcoholic beverages. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. In addition to refilling her prescription for alendronate, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: Schedule a follow-up DEXA scan now

correctExplanation: Depression screening is a routine preventive health measure recommended for all adults. However, elderly adults are under screened for depression. As depression is relatively prevalent in older adults and easily treatable, routine depression screening should occur. Other screening in elderly patients include screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm in men aged 65 to 75 years, breast cancer for women older than age 40 years with a life expectancy more than 5 years, and colorectal cancer for adults older than age 45 years with a life expectancy greater than 5 years. This patient is advanced in age, so cancer screenings are unlikely to be beneficial. Patients older than age 65 years should also be counseled about a healthy lifestyle, including regular aerobic exercise, a diet heavy in healthy fats, and smoking cessation.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Obtain serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration (Choice B) is not a routine screening test in older patients. Also, thyroid-stimulating hormone derangements are likely to present with physical examination findings such as skin or hair changes. This patient's physical examination disclosed no abnormalities.

Order mammography (Choice C) is unlikely to be beneficial in patients with a life expectancy of less than 5 years. Many patients with breast cancer, especially in the early stages, survive longer than 5 years. This patient's advanced age makes breast cancer screening unlikely to be helpful.

Order mental status examination (Choice D) is incorrect. Any physician can perform a mental status examination. Physicians should regularly monitor their patients' mental status for behavior, affect, mood, and cognitive changes. No order is needed for this patient.

Schedule a follow-up DEXA scan now (Choice E) is not necessary. DEXA scans should be repeated every 2 years for patients with osteopenia or osteoporosis. This patient had a relatively recent DEXA scan.

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of decreased appetite, nausea, and occasional vomiting. She also reports fullness and discomfort in her abdomen and abdominal cramps that have awakened her on several occasions. Her last bowel movement was 5 days ago and was characterized by loose stool. Thirty years ago, she underwent hysterectomy for leiomyomata uteri. She has a 10-year history of intermittent urinary incontinence. Her only medication is oxybutynin. Colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities. She appears frail. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 57 kg (125 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min and regular, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Examination shows warm, dry skin. The lungs are clear to auscultation and percussion. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs. The abdomen is soft and diffusely tender; there is no rebound or organomegaly. Rectal examination shows firm stool in the rectal vault. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
correctExplanation: Loose stool in the setting of hard stool in the rectal vault and increased stool burden suggests overflow diarrhea in the setting of severe constipation. Chronic, severe constipation with fecal impaction in the rectum can occur in the setting of decreased mobility, opiate use, or anticholinergic (eg, oxybutynin) use, which suppresses bowel peristalsis and increases the risk for constipation. This patient's episode of loose stool occurred because only liquid can pass adjacent to the impacted stool. The first-line treatment for severe constipation with fecal impaction is administration of an enema. This works by introducing fluid into the large bowel, which serves to expand the intestinal tract lumen, soften the impacted stool, and stimulate peristalsis. Modification of risk factors should also occur, such as increasing fiber in the diet, limiting the use of opiate medications, or introducing stool softeners or osmotic agents into the medication regimen.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, and F.

Adhesions (Choice A) are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in a patient with a history of prior intra-abdominal surgery. Obstruction of the small bowel occurs from partial or complete blockage of the small bowel lumen and typically presents with nausea, vomiting, constipation, obstipation, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension. This patient has a soft abdomen without distension, making small bowel obstruction less likely. Firm stool in the rectal vault is more suggestive of fecal impaction.

Colon cancer (Choice B) most commonly occurs in the rectosigmoid region of the large bowel. Lesions within the ascending colon, by convention, typically result in slow bleeding, leading to iron deficiency anemia. Cancers within the descending and rectosigmoid colon are more likely to be infiltrative, resulting in obstruction of the large bowel. Patients may have thin-appearing stool. Loose stool with firm stool in the rectal vault is more suggestive of fecal impaction. In this patient with a normal colonoscopy 3 years ago, colon cancer so severe to cause constipation is unlikely.

Diverticulitis (Choice C) presents with left lower quadrant abdominal pain, sometimes accompanied by diarrhea, fever, and tenderness to palpation over the left lower quadrant. Ischemic bowel (Choice E), such as with ischemic colitis, refers to inadequate blood supply to the colon, which can lead to bowel wall necrosis, loss of immune barriers, and bowel perforation. Ischemic colitis most commonly occurs in the setting of atherosclerosis, resulting in plaque rupture within a mesenteric vessel, systemic hypotension (eg, shock), or emboli such as in atrial fibrillation. Typical symptoms of patients with acute ischemic colitis include crampy abdominal pain, tenderness over the affected bowel, and hematochezia. This patient does not have focal tenderness, hematochezia, or risk factors for ischemic colitis, making this diagnosis less likely.

Volvulus (Choice F) such as sigmoid volvulus results from twisting of the sigmoid mesentery, which can lead to large bowel obstruction and potential rupture or intestinal necrosis if not treated. It typically shows a coffee-bean appearance on abdominal x-rays. Sigmoid volvulus generally presents in an older patient with increasing abdominal distention, abdominal pain, constipation, and possible obstipation. This patient has a soft abdomen without distension and a sensation of fullness and discomfort, not severe abdominal pain, making sigmoid volvulus less likely.

questionStem: A 24-year-old man comes to the office due to a 2-day history of dysuria and urethral discharge. He has had multiple sexual partners and does not consistently use condoms. He was treated for a similar episode 6 months ago. Physical examination shows a purulent urethral discharge. Gram stain of the discharge shows numerous neutrophils but no organisms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: This patient should receive testing for Chlamydia trachomatis given his history of previous infection and unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners. C. trachomatis is a sexually transmitted infection that classically presents in men with urethritis, dysuria, and urethral discharge. However, it can also be asymptomatic. For this reason, testing for C. trachomatis, as well as for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is recommended by the United States Preventive Services Task Force for all sexually active patients under age 25 years. Complications of undiagnosed infection in men include epididymitis and reactive arthritis, as well as the possibility of further transmission to additional partners. Diagnosis is made with a nucleic acid amplification test, and treatment consists of either azithromycin or doxycycline in combination with ceftriaxone, with the latter covering a potential N. gonorrhoeae coinfection. The risk for reinfection in patients previously treated for C. trachomatis is high. As such, patients should be retested approximately 3 months after treatment to ensure their infection has resolved and they have not been reinfected.
incorrectExplanation: Herpes simplex virus, type 1 (Choice B) is most commonly characterized by tender vesicles followed by ulceration and crusting, more frequently around the mouth, whereas herpes simplex virus, type 2 (Choice C) is more frequently characterized by similar lesions on the genitalia. Other symptoms of genital herpes include dysuria. Diagnosis of herpes can be clinical given the classic appearance of the infection, or via viral culture of any vesicles. Routine testing is less meaningful and not frequently performed, as many patients have positive serologic studies for herpes but no evidence of active or treatable infection. Human papillomavirus (Choice D) is a sexually transmitted viral infection that can cause cervical/vulvar and penile/anal carcinoma, as well as condyloma acuminata. Testing for human papillomavirus can be done in conjunction with Pap smear cytology in women but is not a part of routine diagnosis for active sexually transmitted infections, as many patients will have transient infections that clear on their own. No further testing is indicated (Choice E) is incorrect. This patient was previously infected with a sexually transmitted infection and continues to have unprotected sexual intercourse. He is at increased risk for reinfection with C. trachomatis or a new infection with N. gonorrhoeae or HIV. He should therefore undergo testing for these sexually transmitted infections in order to prevent the sequelae of disease or further transmission to future partners.

questionStem: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension comes to the physician for a routine examination. Six months ago following a myocardial infarction, he underwent coronary artery bypass grafting that involved harvesting of the saphenous vein. He says he feels well. His medications are metformin, metoprolol, and lisinopril. Before his operation, he walked 3 miles daily; he has not resumed walking because he says he lacks the desire. On further questioning, he says he has not resumed any social activities because he feels tired on most days and does not want to leave his house. His blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg; other vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, there is lower extremity edema bilaterally, which is worse on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Administration of the Geriatric Depression Scale
choices.D: Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities

correctExplanation: This patient is likely to meet criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD). Symptoms of MDD include 2 or more weeks of at least five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia (eg, decreased interest in exercising or socializing), guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor slowing or agitation, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (eg, decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. This patient demonstrates anhedonia and decreased energy despite his recovery from surgery several months ago. Though some patients are able to express a depressed mood, others (particularly men, patients over the age of 65 years, and African American patients) may not initially report a depressed mood and/or may present with primarily somatic symptoms. Treatment of MDD should include psychotherapy and antidepressant medication.
incorrectExplanation:
Determination of ankle brachial indices (Choice B) would assist in diagnosing peripheral artery disease (PAD). PAD commonly presents with extremity pain with activity and weak pulses. Edema, as seen in this patient, is uncommon. Also, this patient demonstrates a constellation of symptoms consistent with MDD.

Determination of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (Choice C) would assist in assessing for systemic inflammation. Though erythrocyte sedimentation rate is commonly measured in patients presenting with fatigue who have other focal symptoms that indicate an inflammatory process (eg, joint pain), this patient’s fatigue is likely caused by MDD as he has multiple symptoms suggestive of MDD. He does not report focal symptoms other than pedal edema, which is a known complication of coronary artery bypass surgery involving saphenous vein harvesting.

Doppler ultrasonography of the lower extremities (Choice D) assists in diagnosing deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Symptoms and signs include unilateral lower extremity edema, skin pigmentation changes, pain, vein dilation, and venous ulcer formation. This patient shows bilateral pedal edema and lacks other typical signs of DVT. Fatigue and anhedonia are not common DVT symptoms.

Echocardiography (Choice E) can be used to evaluate for systolic or diastolic dysfunction, intravascular volume status, and pericardial effusion. It is commonly used to determine the severity of a patient’s heart failure. This patient’s blood pressure is well controlled, and he does not have symptoms of heart failure (eg, dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea).

Determination of ankle brachial indices (Choice B) would assist in diagnosing peripheral artery disease (PAD). PAD commonly presents with extremity pain with activity and weak pulses. Echocardiography (Choice E) can be used to evaluate for systolic or diastolic dysfunction, intravascular volume status, and pericardial effusion. It is commonly used to determine the severity of a patient’s heart failure. Though bilateral pedal edema is a sign of heart failure exacerbation, this patient feels physically well and does not report symptoms of heart failure, such as dyspnea or orthopnea.
