questionStem: Of 65 men with coronary artery disease, 38 had an abnormal exercise stress test. Which of the following characteristics of screening tests does this demonstrate?

choices.C: Predictive value of a positive test

correctExplanation: Sensitivity is the ability of a test to detect a disease if it is present. A test is described as sensitive if it has a high likelihood of disease detection and, therefore, a low likelihood of a false negative (type 2 error). Given that the majority of patients with an abnormal exercise stress test have a history of coronary artery disease, the exercise stress test is a relatively sensitive measure of coronary artery disease. High sensitivity is therefore useful in ruling out a disease because a negative result indicates a very low likelihood that the disease is present. Because of this, high-sensitivity tests are useful for screening purposes in which proving the absence of disease and limiting the number of false-negative results are of the utmost importance. Sensitivity can be calculated by dividing true positives (TP) by the sum of TP and false negatives (FN), or TP/(TP + FN).
incorrectExplanation: False-negative rate (Choice A) refers to the proportion of patients with negative stress tests who do in fact have coronary artery disease. Likelihood ratio (Choice B) is the ratio of false results to true results. Negative likelihood ratio is the ratio of false negatives to true negatives, while positive likelihood ratio is the ratio of false positives to true positives. This vignette does not describe false positives or negatives and instead identifies the proportion of true positives with a positive test result, which is consistent with sensitivity. Predictive value of a positive test (Choice C) is a statistical measure that defines the proportion of positive test results that are true positives (positive tests in patients who have the condition). Instead, this vignette describes the number of true positives (patients with coronary artery disease) who had positive test results. This is a separate concept more consistent with sensitivity. Specificity (Choice E) describes the proportion of people who do not have the disease who test negative and is calculated as: true negatives / (true negatives + false positives). As specificity increases, the false-positive rate decreases. This vignette instead describes the proportion of true positives who test positive on the screening test, consistent with sensitivity.

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She says that she began following a vegan diet (no dairy or animal products) 2 months ago. She takes no medications or dietary supplements. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Supplementation with which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?
correctExplanation: In this patient who has recently converted to a vegan diet, it is most appropriate to begin supplementation with calcium. Patients who follow vegan diets are at increased risk for deficiencies of iron, calcium, zinc, protein, fatty acids, and vitamin B12 (cobalamin). Given that these patients do not have consistent intake of these essential vitamins and minerals, it is appropriate to begin supplementation even prior to the emergence of any symptoms or signs of deficiency. In these patients, the low intake of dietary calcium increases the total body concentration of parathyroid hormone as well as vitamin D. This causes a reuptake of calcium from the bones to maintain appropriate serum concentrations. Over time, this can lead to low bone density and subsequent pathologic fractures.
incorrectExplanation:
Folic acid (Choice B) supplementation is not necessary at this time. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for folate deficiency. This is because high concentrations of folate can be found in green leafy vegetables, which the patient is regularly consuming.

Magnesium (Choice C) supplementation is not necessary at this time. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for magnesium deficiency. This is because high concentrations of magnesium can be found in green leafy vegetables, beans, kale, spinach, bananas, and avocados.

Manganese (Choice D) supplementation is not necessary in this patient. Patients who follow vegan or vegetarian diets are not generally at risk for manganese deficiency. This is because many foods that are part of these diets are high in manganese. Some examples of these are whole grains, quinoa, almonds, hazelnuts, chickpeas, spinach, and tofu.

questionStem: A 38-year-old woman has had an 8-day history of malaise, sore throat, nasal congestion, and rhinitis and a 2-day history of temperatures to 40°C (104°F), shortness of breath, and cough productive of yellow mucus. She is alert and oriented. Her temperature is 39.7°C (103.4°F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 108/72 mm Hg. Breath sounds are decreased at the left apex posteriorly and anteriorly with increased tactile fremitus over that area. Inspiratory and expiratory crackles and rhonchi are heard. There is a normal S1 and S2 and no cyanosis, clubbing, or pedal edema. Her leukocyte count is 16,000/mm³. An x-ray of the chest shows a left upper lobe consolidation. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus and is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia. Typical signs of pneumococcal pneumonia include fever, chills, productive cough, shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain. Vital signs may show tachycardia and tachypnea. Physical examination may show rhonchi, crackles, decreased breath sounds, and increased tactile fremitus, such as in this patient. X-rays commonly show a lobar consolidation or, less commonly, bronchopneumonia. Management of community-acquired pneumonia includes antibiotics. Depending on severity and patient risk factors, the condition may require supplemental oxygen or mechanical respiratory support, intravenous antibiotics, and admission. Acute bacterial pneumonia may occur in isolation or following a viral respiratory syndrome, as in this case.
incorrectExplanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Choice A) presents with hilar adenopathy and calcified pulmonary granulomas in primary infection. In reactivation, patients present with apical pulmonary opacities and fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis. This patient does not have night sweats or risk factors for tuberculosis infection, making this an unlikely causal organism.

questionStem: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, cough, and shortness of breath. He has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is a current smoker. His temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 24/min. On examination, he is in moderate respiratory distress. Lung auscultation reveals crackles in the right lower lung field. A chest x-ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia. X-rays often show a lobar consolidation. Treatment includes antibiotics and supportive care measures.

questionStem: A 45-year-old man with gout has the sudden onset of extreme pain, swelling, and exquisite tenderness of the right knee; he cannot bear the pressure of wearing slacks. He has not recently taken any medication and previously had intractable diarrhea while taking colchicine. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for treating this acute episode?
correctExplanation: Gout is an acute, monoarticular arthropathy resulting from an intra-articular inflammatory reaction to precipitation of monosodium urate crystals. Deposition of uric acid crystals may occur in the surrounding tissues, leading to the development of tophi. Gout typically presents with atraumatic joint pain, erythema, and swelling. The most common joint involved is the first metatarsophalangeal, but other common joints include the knees and elbows. Treatment of an acute flare consists of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as naproxen or indomethacin as well as colchicine, or corticosteroids. In this case, the patient is most likely presenting with a gout flare because of the sudden onset of his symptoms. The most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy is indomethacin for this patient who previously did not tolerate colchicine.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, D, and E.

Allopurinol (Choice A) and probenecid (Choice E) are both urate-lowering medications. Allopurinol functions by inhibiting xanthine oxidase and probenecid functions by decreasing the reabsorption of urate. These medications are important pharmacological options in preventing gout flares. In this case, the patient is presenting with an acute gout flare.

Codeine (Choice B) is an opiate medication used for pain management or cough in a select group of patients. In cases of acute gout flares, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and/or corticosteroids are the first-line treatments for pain relief and management. Indomethacin would be the most appropriate drug for treating this acute gout flare.

Prednisone (Choice D) is often not the most recommended initial therapy for the treatment of an acute gout flare. Because of its side effect profile, most clinicians recommend the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or colchicine initially. While steroids can be given for acute gout flares, these other medications are typically administered first.

questionStem: A 72-year-old African American man comes to the office because of a 2-day history of mild, vague abdominal pain. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and osteoarthritis of the knees. His medications are lisinopril, metformin, and acetaminophen. He does not smoke cigarettes or use illicit drugs. He drinks eight glasses of wine weekly. He is a retired hotel desk clerk. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 79 kg (175 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 156/97 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a pulsatile midline mass 7 cm above the umbilicus. No other abnormalities are noted. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin A1c of 8.4% and serum total cholesterol concentration of 260 mg/dL. Which of the following factors is most predictive of future complications of this patient’s condition?
correctExplanation: This older patient with a pulsatile abdominal mass has examination findings consistent with an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). AAAs are most commonly seen in male smokers with a family or personal history of atherosclerotic disease. They commonly occur in the infrarenal abdominal aorta and may present as a palpable, pulsatile abdominal mass if the aneurysm is large and the patient is a healthy weight. Smoking is the modifiable risk factor most strongly associated with both development of an AAA as well as its expansion and rupture. Uncontrolled hypertension has been shown to be associated with increased rate of expansion and rupture as well, although the association is less strong. Ruptured aneurysms require emergent surgical intervention and repair. Chronic aneurysms are typically asymptomatic. The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends using ultrasonography to screen for AAA in men age 65 to 75 years who have a history of tobacco use.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, and E.

Alcohol consumption (Choice A) has variable effects on AAA development. Small amounts of moderate alcohol consumption have been shown to reduce risk for AAA development, while high levels (more than 2 drinks/day) of alcohol consumption may slightly increase the risk. This patient has a moderate level of alcohol consumption, which would not contribute to his risk for developing an AAA and may even be protective. Alcohol consumption has not been shown to affect the rate of AAA rupture.

Ethnicity (Choice C) has been associated with the prevalence of AAA, but not with risk for rupture or expansion. AAAs develop most frequently in White patients; however, AAA can develop in patients of any ethnicity.

Hemoglobin A1c measurement (Choice D) would not be predictive of future complications in this patient. Diabetes is associated with a lower risk for the development of an AAA, as well as AAA expansion and rupture.

Serum total cholesterol concentration (Choice E) does contribute to the development of an AAA, but there is no association between hyperlipidemia and AAA expansion and rupture.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of frequent loss of urine. During this time, she has had loss of urine at rest and with activity. She wears an absorbent pad each night; it is soaked by morning. She has difficulty initiating her urinary stream, which is weak. She has had six urinary tract infections during the past year. She has had type 1 diabetes mellitus since the age of 6 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A cough stress test is positive. Her postvoid residual volume is 800 mL. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Overflow incontinence occurs when bladder emptying is impaired, eventually resulting in intravesical hydrostatic pressure overcoming internal and external urinary sphincter closing pressures, thereby causing the leakage of urine. It can occur due to a variety of causes, including neurologic insults (eg, diabetic neuropathy, stroke, trauma, multiple sclerosis) that result in bladder atony, and bladder outlet obstruction secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia or a bladder mass. This patient's long history of type 1 diabetes mellitus increases her risk for diabetic neuropathy and overflow incontinence secondary to neurogenic bladder. Patients develop urinary retention with an inability to void and may have loss of urine with Valsalva maneuver or increased abdominopelvic pressure. The diagnosis is established with a urodynamic study, which typically shows an increased postvoid residual volume, such as in this patient with a postvoid residual volume of 800 mL. In contrast to an overactive bladder, which is treated with oxybutynin, overflow incontinence is treated with bethanechol, a muscarinic agent that promotes bladder contraction, or with intermittent catheterization.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, C, D, E, and F. Functional incontinence (Choice A) describes incontinence secondary to external factors or another condition creating inability to void in a timely manner or inability to recognize the need to void. Several causes of functional incontinence include cognitive disorders such as dementia, movement disorders such as multiple sclerosis or Parkinson disease, physical barriers, or medication effect. This patient has no evidence of a secondary cause of incontinence. Rather, she shows signs of a primary cause of incontinence, overflow incontinence, as evidenced by increased postvoid residual volume. Stress incontinence (Choice C) is incontinence that is triggered by an increase in intra-abdominal pressure (eg, lifting, sneezing, Valsalva maneuver). Stress incontinence results from urethral hypermobility caused by pelvic floor weakness/prolapse or intrinsic sphincter deficiency. Urethral hypermobility is evidenced on physical examination by deviation greater than 30 degrees from the horizontal of an inserted cotton-tipped applicator with straining. This patient's physical examination is normal, making stress incontinence less likely. In addition, stress incontinence would not have increased postvoid residual volume, which is more suggestive of overflow incontinence. Risk factors for stress incontinence include multiple vaginal deliveries, obesity, and prostate surgery.

questionStem: A 62-year-old man comes to the office due to urinary incontinence. He has a long history of type 1 diabetes mellitus complicated by retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy. The patient has had several episodes of urinary tract infections over the past year. He has no dysuria or hematuria. The patient voids small amounts of urine frequently and has a weak urinary stream. He also has nocturia. On physical examination, the bladder is palpable above the pubic symphysis. Postvoid residual volume is 800 mL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's incontinence?
correctExplanation: Overflow incontinence occurs when bladder emptying is impaired, eventually resulting in intravesical hydrostatic pressure overcoming internal and external urinary sphincter closing pressures, thereby causing the leakage of urine. It can occur due to a variety of causes, including neurologic insults (eg, diabetic neuropathy, stroke, trauma, multiple sclerosis) that result in bladder atony, and bladder outlet obstruction secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia or a bladder mass. This patient's long history of type 1 diabetes mellitus increases his risk for diabetic neuropathy and overflow incontinence secondary to neurogenic bladder. Patients develop urinary retention and may have loss of urine with Valsalva maneuvers or increased abdominopelvic pressure. The diagnosis is established with a urodynamic study, which typically shows an increased postvoid residual volume, such as in this patient with a postvoid residual volume of 800 mL. In contrast to an overactive bladder, which is treated with oxybutynin, overflow incontinence is treated with bethanechol, a muscarinic agent that promotes bladder contraction, or with intermittent catheterization.
incorrectExplanation:
Functional incontinence (Choice A) describes incontinence secondary to external factors or another condition creating inability to void in a timely manner or inability to recognize the need to void. Several causes of functional incontinence include cognitive or physical impairments such as dementia, movement disorders such as multiple sclerosis or Parkinson disease, physical barriers, or medication effect. This patient has no evidence of a secondary cause of incontinence. Rather, she shows signs of a primary cause of incontinence, overflow incontinence, as evidenced by increased postvoid residual volume.

Stress incontinence (Choice C) is incontinence that is triggered by an increase in intra-abdominal pressure (eg, lifting, sneezing, Valsalva maneuver). Stress incontinence results from urethral hypermobility caused by pelvic floor weakness/prolapse or intrinsic sphincter deficiency. Urethral hypermobility is evidenced on physical examination by deviation greater than 30 degrees from the horizontal of an inserted cotton-tipped applicator with straining. This patient's physical examination is normal, making stress incontinence less likely. In addition, stress incontinence would not have increased postvoid residual volume, which is more suggestive of overflow incontinence. Risk factors for stress incontinence include multiple vaginal deliveries, obesity, and prostate surgery.

Urge incontinence (Choice D), or overactive bladder with incontinence, is caused by detrusor muscle instability and commonly presents with the urge to void followed shortly by the leakage of urine. Patients would have low postvoid residual volume, in contrast with overflow incontinence such as in this patient. Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic medication used to treat urge incontinence from an overactive bladder and detrusor instability.

Urinary tract infection (Choice E) can present with an overactive bladder (frequency, urgency, urge incontinence). Patients generally also experience dysuria and suprapubic pain. The presence of bacteria and white blood cells on urinalysis is typical. This patient has no dysuria and a normal urinalysis, making urinary tract infection unlikely.

Vesicovaginal fistula (Choice F) can be a consequence of gynecologic surgery, pelvic malignancy, or radiation therapy. It typically presents with painless urinary leakage from the bladder into the vagina. On pelvic examination, a pool of urine is typically present in the vaginal canal. This patient's physical examination shows no abnormalities, making vesicovaginal fistula less likely.

questionStem: A 20-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine health maintenance examination. She says she feels well. She has no history of serious illness or sexually transmitted infection. Her only medication is an oral contraceptive, for which she requests a refill. She has had five lifetime sexual partners. During the past 4 months, she has been monogamous with one male partner. She has never used condoms. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. In addition to refilling the oral contraceptive prescription, which of the following is the most appropriate screening for cervical cancer?

choices.B: Pap smear and high-risk HPV genotyping
choices.C: Pap smear with reflex HPV testing
choices.E: No screening is indicated at this time

correctExplanation: No cervical cancer screening is indicated at this patient's age. Pap smear testing uses a cervical swab to collect cells from the transformation zone of the cervix and is an important screening tool for the detection of cervical carcinoma. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) guidelines recommend screening for cervical carcinoma with Pap smear testing every 3 years between ages 21 and 29 years, and Pap smear screening every 5 years with co-testing for human papillomavirus (HPV) or every 3 years with Pap smear testing alone between ages 30 and 65 years. Screening is not recommended before age 21 years. However, this patient should undergo appropriate screening for sexually transmitted infections, such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, given her history of unprotected intercourse with multiple prior partners.
incorrectExplanation: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) genotyping only (Choice A) is not recommended as a screening modality for sexually transmitted infections or cervical cancer. The strains most commonly implicated in condyloma acuminata are HPV 6 and 11, whereas those that confer the highest risk for progression to cervical cancer include strains 16, 18, 31, and 33. Screening in asymptomatic patients is not recommended as infections are typically transient and may be cleared by the patient’s immune system. Pap smear and high-risk HPV genotyping (Choice B) is not recommended for this patient. Pap smear and high-risk HPV genotyping is typically reserved as a cervical cancer screening modality for patients between ages 30 and 65 years. Screening is not recommended in patients under age 21 years.

questionStem: A 28-year-old woman, who was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus 1 month ago, comes to the office as a new patient. She recently moved to the area. The diagnosis was made based on a 2-week history of excessive urination and a nonfasting serum glucose concentration of 225 mg/dL. She is currently asymptomatic. She has no other history of serious illness. Her only medication is metformin. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Today, her hemoglobin A1c is 6.1%, and nonfasting serum glucose concentration is 135 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient to prevent disease-related morbidity?
correctExplanation: The 2023 United States Preventive Services Task Force guidelines recommend various screening tests and interventions for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Comprehensive eye examination, foot examination, major depressive disorder screening, weight management counseling, and tobacco cessation counseling are recommended annually. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus should also be screened for high blood pressure at every medical visit. Lipid profile screening should be done at least every 5 years to measure total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides concentrations. Annual urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio test and blood test to measure serum creatinine concentration should be performed to detect early-stage kidney disease. Guidelines may need to be individualized based on a patient's specific clinical characteristics and comorbidities.
incorrectExplanation:
Exercise stress test (Choice B) is not appropriate for this patient. While patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus do have increased risk for cardiovascular disease, this patient shows no signs or symptoms of this. Additionally, this patient has no complaints of chest pain, nor ECG findings that would be suggestive of unstable angina or any type of occlusive coronary lesion.

Herpes zoster vaccination (Choice C) is not necessary for this patient. Herpes zoster vaccination is recommended for immunocompetent individuals over the age of 50. Given the patient's age and lack of history of HIV, cancer, or autoimmune disease, this is not required.

Monthly determination of hemoglobin A1c (Choice D) is not appropriate. Hemoglobin A1c is a measurement of average glycosylation of red blood cells (RBCs). Given that the average lifespan of RBCs is 90-120 days, it gives a reliable estimate of average blood glucose concentration over the preceding three months. Monthly checks are not appropriate, even in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Pneumococcal vaccination (Choice E) is not necessary for this patient. Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for patients over the age of 65 or for patients who are asplenic. Given this patient's age and lack of history of splenectomy, this is incorrect.

Additionally, this patient has no complaints of chest pain, nor ECG findings that would be suggestive of unstable angina or any type of occlusive coronary lesion.

Herpes zoster vaccination (Choice C) is not necessary for this patient. Herpes zoster vaccination is recommended for immunocompetent individuals over the age of 50. Given the patient's age and lack of history of HIV, cancer, or autoimmune disease, this is not yet required.

Monthly determination of hemoglobin A1c (Choice D) is not appropriate. Hemoglobin A1c is a measurement of average glycosylation of red blood cells (RBCs). Given that the average lifespan of RBCs is 90-120 days, it gives a reliable estimate of average blood glucose concentration over the preceding three months. Monthly checks are not appropriate, even in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Pneumococcal vaccination (Choice E) is not necessary for this patient. Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for patients over the age of 65 or for patients who are asplenic. Given this patient's age and lack of history of splenectomy, this is incorrect.

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because of a 6-month history of moderate right upper abdominal pain that occurs 15 to 60 minutes after he eats. The episodes occur once or twice weekly and resolve in less than 1 hour. He otherwise is asymptomatic. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. His mother says he eats three fast-food meals weekly. Growth and development are appropriate for age. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is nontender. The spleen tip is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows 20 gallstones measuring 3 mm to 10 mm. His hemoglobin concentration is 7.7 g/dL (N=11.5–14.5). A blood smear shows spherocytes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

choices.A: Change in the shape of red blood cells
choices.D: Production of autoantibodies directed against the red blood cell membrane
choices.E: Switch from glutamic acid to valine in the globin chain

correctExplanation: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is a disorder of red blood cell membrane proteins that limits the ability of the cell to conform when passing through narrow capillary beds. This results in early removal of the red blood cells by the spleen and a resultant hemolysis, which causes normocytic, hemolytic anemia. HS is the most common disorder of the red blood cell membrane and is frequently seen in people of European descent. A family history of HS is generally present. Autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins cause HS through loss of the normal connection between the inner membrane skeleton and the outer lipid bilayer. Patients typically present with fatigue, global weakness, and pallor, with associated splenomegaly and jaundice on physical examination. Laboratory studies generally show an increased indirect hyperbilirubinemia along with an abnormal osmotic fragility test and eosin-5’-maleimide analysis on flow cytometry. Patients are prone to development of bilirubin gallstones because of the high levels of indirect bilirubin. Blood smear shows rounded red blood cells without central pallor. Splenic congestion and sequestration are hallmarks of moderate -to -severe disease. Splenectomy is indicated to reduce the degree of premature red blood cell consumption (ie, extravascular hemolysis) and the risk for sequestration crises.
incorrectExplanation:
A fat-rich diet (Choice B) is not the most likely cause. While this patient does have evidence of cholelithiasis, which can then precipitate pain after fatty meals, he also has 20 gallstones which is significantly abnormal. In addition, this patient has spherocytes on blood smear and splenomegaly, neither of which can be attributed to a fat-rich diet.

Presence of antiplatelet IgG antibodies (Choice C) is seen in immune thrombocytopenia, which results from the immune-mediated destruction of circulating platelets. It presents with thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding (eg, petechiae, purpura, epistaxis) rather than hemolytic anemia.

Production of autoantibodies directed against the red blood cell membrane (Choice D) is seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). AIHA is characterized by the presence of spherocytes on peripheral blood smear and a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test. However, AIHA is not associated with gallstones.

Switch from glutamic acid to valine in the globin chain (Choice E) is seen in sickle cell disease, which is characterized by hemolytic anemia and vaso-occlusive pain crises. This patient has no history of pain crises and has spherocytes rather than sickled cells on blood smear.

questionStem: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician due to 2 weeks of fatigue and dark urine. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. The patient is of Northern European descent. Laboratory results are as follows: Hemoglobin: 10.8 g/dL, Reticulocytes: 8%, Total bilirubin: 4.2 mg/dL, Direct bilirubin: 0.4 mg/dL, Lactate dehydrogenase: 220 U/L, Haptoglobin: 20 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear shows numerous spherocytes. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

choices.A: Defective binding of red blood cell cytoskeleton to plasma membrane

Clinical symptoms include jaundice, splenomegaly, and anemia, along with the presence of pigmented gallstones. Peripheral smear shows normocytic, normochromic anemia with the presence of spherocytes. Definitive treatment is with splenectomy.

In addition, this patient has spherocytes on blood smear and splenomegaly, neither of which can be attributed to a fat-rich diet. Presence of antiplatelet IgG antibodies (Choice C) is seen in immune thrombocytopenia, which results from the immune-mediated destruction of circulating platelets. It presents with thrombocytopenia, mucosal bleeding, and petechiae or purpura from cutaneous hemorrhage. Platelets and erythrocytes appear normal on peripheral smear, making this answer unlikely. Production of autoantibodies directed against the red blood cell membrane (Choice D) is seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is a type II (complement-mediated cytotoxicity) hypersensitivity reaction in which autoantibodies form to antigens on the surface of erythrocytes. questionStem: A 65-year-old man comes to the office due to a skin lesion on his face. The lesion has been present for several months and has slowly increased in size. Physical examination shows a 1.5-cm pearly nodule with rolled borders and overlying telangiectasia on the left cheek. The lesion is excised, and pathology shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common subtype of skin cancer and is associated with ultraviolet (UV) exposure. Basal cell carcinoma clinically presents as a pearly papule with rolled borders, overlying telangiectasia, and may have focal erosion or ulceration. Patients often describe this lesion as 'the pimple that will not pop' or 'the wound that will not heal.' Basal cell carcinoma can be locally invasive; however, metastasis is rare. Clinical subtypes of basal cell carcinoma include nodular, pigmented, morpheaform, and micronodular. Basal cell carcinoma pathology will show islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading, and retraction from the surrounding dermis. Treatment for basal cell carcinoma includes excision such as Mohs micrographic surgery, electrodesiccation and curettage, or topical imiquimod therapy. This patient’s presentation and the photograph shown are consistent with basal cell carcinoma.
incorrectExplanation:
Actinic keratoses (Choice A) are associated with UV damage and are found on sun-exposed sites including the face, ears, neck, and extremities. Actinic keratoses result from partial-thickness epidermal atypia, which may progress to squamous cell carcinoma if left untreated. Physical examination discloses ill-defined, rough, scaly papules. Actinic keratoses are treated with cryotherapy, topical fluorouracil, and topical imiquimod. While actinic keratoses are associated with UV damage, this case is more consistent with basal cell carcinoma.

Keratocanthoma (Choice C) is considered a variant of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Keratoacanthoma clinically presents as a rapidly enlarging, crateriform nodule, with a central hyperkeratotic core. Keratoacanthoma, unlike squamous cell carcinoma, may involute over a period of months, leaving behind a scar. While some lesions spontaneously resolve, biopsy is recommended to rule out invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Keratoacanthoma usually shows rapid growth, unlike a slow growing basal cell carcinoma.

Seborrheic keratosis (Choice D) is a common benign growth, found in middle-aged and elderly adults. They commonly present as brown, sharply demarcated papules in sun-exposed sites. Seborrheic keratoses do not represent melanocytic growths, but are related to a thickening of the epidermis, pigment deposition, and development of intraepidermal keratin cysts. Patients should be provided reassurance. Seborrheic keratoses may be clinically monitored.

Squamous cell carcinoma (Choice E) is the second most common form of skin cancer and is associated with chronic sun exposure. UV damage over time leads to the development of thymidine dimers and mutations in p53, a tumor suppressor gene. Squamous cell carcinoma clinically presents as a chronic, rough, eroded papule or nodule, with an overlying hyperkeratotic crust. Lesions suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma warrant biopsy, and treatment modalities include standard excision, Mohs micrographic surgery, and electrodesiccation and curettage. This case is consistent with basal cell carcinoma.

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 3-week history of nausea without associated vomiting. The patient's mother waits outside the examination room during the evaluation. The patient has no history of serious medical illness and takes no medications. Since menarche at age 11 years, her menstrual periods have occurred at irregular 30- to 60-day intervals; her last menstrual period was 2 months ago. The patient reports that she has been dating her 18-year-old boyfriend for the past 5 months; they are sexually active and use condoms inconsistently. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.4°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urine pregnancy test is positive. While discussing the results with the patient, she states that she does not know what to do. Which of the following is the most important question for the physician to ask the patient during the conversation?

choices.A: Do you want me to contact child protective services?
choices.B: Have you considered placing the child up for adoption?
choices.C: How do you think your boyfriend will react to this news?
choices.D: Is this a situation we could discuss with your mother?
choices.E: Would you like a confidential referral to discuss abortion services?

correctExplanation: Parental consent is required for most medical care of minors (patients younger than 18 years). Exceptions include medical care related to sexual health (eg, pregnancy care, sexually transmitted infection, contraception), substance use, and life-threatening or psychiatric conditions. For these sensitive or time-sensitive issues, patient confidentiality and autonomy is favored over other ethical principles. This minor patient who is pregnant has challenging decisions to make. The physician's role is to discuss the options and facilitate informed and thoughtful decisions. She should be asked whether she wants her parents involved in the decision-making. If she expresses a preference to exclude her parents, the physician should honor her preference.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

“Do you want me to contact child protective services?” (Choice A) is not a question a physician should ask a patient. As a mandated reporter, the physician is required by law to report any suspected child abuse. There is no indication that the boyfriend or parents are abusing this patient or that this patient is a danger to the fetus.

“Have you considered placing the child up for adoption?” (Choice B) and “Would you like a confidential referral to discuss abortion services?” (Choice E) are leading questions that presume that one is the best option. The decision of whether to deliver and raise a child is a personal decision. The physician should facilitate discussion of the options while abstaining from expressing an opinion.

“How do you think your boyfriend will react to this news?” (Choice C) strays from the physician’s role of facilitating informed decision-making about management options. Though the physician may encourage the patient to discuss the decision with her loved ones (including her boyfriend) so she can think through her decision, the boyfriend’s reaction is irrelevant. Additionally, this question may come off as judgmental.

questionStem: A previously healthy 82-year-old woman comes to the physician because of generalized weakness and a sore tongue for 1 month. She lives by herself. Her diet has consisted mainly of tea and homemade bread since her husband died 6 months ago. Examination shows pallor, mild jaundice, and a smooth, red tongue. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 26%, Mean corpuscular volume 120 μm³, Leukocyte count 2500/mm³, Reticulocyte count 0.2%, Platelet count 20,000/mm³. This patient most likely has which of the following nutritional deficiencies?
correctExplanation: Folic acid, or vitamin B₉, is converted in the body to tetrahydrofolic acid and used as a coenzyme in the synthesis of nucleotides and nucleosides. Folate is contained in leafy vegetables and primarily absorbed in the jejunum. Folate deficiency is often seen in patients with malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, and patients taking anti-folate medications (eg, phenytoin, methotrexate). Megaloblastic anemia occurs in the setting of impaired deoxyribonucleic acid synthesis, commonly related to folate or vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) deficiency, and is classically characterized by erythrocyte macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils. Laboratory studies show anemia, increased mean corpuscular volume, and normal leukocyte and platelet indices. In this patient's case, the megaloblastic anemia is likely a result of folic acid deficiency, as these stores in the body can be depleted quickly in cases of malnourishment, while vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) reserves are substantial and take longer to deplete.
incorrectExplanation: Niacin (Choice B) results in pellagra, which classically presents with the triad of dementia, diarrhea, and dermatitis. The dermatitis is generally seen around a patient's neck in the pattern of a necklace. This patient has not had diarrhea or dermatitis.

questionStem: A 45-year-old man comes to the office due to progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea. He has a history of alcohol use disorder and has been homeless for several years. Physical examination shows pallor and a shiny, smooth tongue. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin level of 9.5 g/dL and mean corpuscular volume of 112 fL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: Folic acid, or vitamin B9, is converted in the body to tetrahydrofolic acid and used as a coenzyme in the synthesis of nucleotides and nucleosides. Folate is contained in leafy vegetables and primarily absorbed in the jejunum. Folate deficiency is often seen in patients with malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, and patients taking anti-folate medications (eg, phenytoin, methotrexate). Megaloblastic anemia occurs in the setting of impaired deoxyribonucleic acid synthesis, commonly related to folate or vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, and is classically characterized by erythrocyte macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils. Laboratory studies show anemia, increased mean corpuscular volume, and normal leukocyte and platelet indices. In this patient's case, the megaloblastic anemia is likely a result of folic acid deficiency, as these stores in the body can be depleted quickly in cases of malnourishment, while vitamin B12 (cobalamin) reserves are substantial and take longer to deplete.
incorrectExplanation: Niacin (Choice B) results in pellagra, which classically presents with the triad of dementia, diarrhea, and dermatitis. The dermatitis is generally seen around a patient's neck in the pattern of a necklace. This patient has not had diarrhea or dermatitis. Deficiency is characterized by Wernicke encephalopathy, a triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. Wernicke encephalopathy is theoretically reversible with administration of high-dose thiamine; if untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome characterized by dementia, confabulation, hallucinations, and psychosis. Vitamin B6 (Choice D) deficiency is uncommon because of dietary insufficiency but when it does occur, it presents as glossitis, stomatitis, and seborrheic dermatitis. It occasionally develops because of chronic therapy with isoniazid for the treatment of tuberculosis and can also result in peripheral neuropathy, but this is typically prevented by prophylactic supplementation with vitamin B6 during the antituberculosis therapy regimen. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (Choice E) deficiency, similar to folic acid deficiency, is classically characterized by erythrocyte macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils. In addition, it also results in posterior column and spinocerebellar tract demyelination. It is most often seen in patients with malnutrition, alcoholism, pernicious anemia, or Crohn disease. However, in this patient who has only been malnourished for approximately 6 months, it is unlikely that these signs are because of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) depletion due to extensive storage in the body and lack of neurologic findings at present.

questionStem: An 82-year-old woman with dementia, Alzheimer type, is brought to the physician by her daughter for recommendations about driving restrictions. Since the patient moved in with her daughter 3 weeks ago, they have had several arguments because her daughter has not allowed the patient to drive. The patient last drove a car 2 years ago. She has no history of motor vehicle collisions. The patient's husband provided her daily care until he died of a myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago. The patient's only medication is galantamine, which she has taken for 4 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status examination shows a sad mood and reactive affect. She reports no suicidal thoughts. She is able to correctly repeat six digits forward, and she recalls one of three objects after 5 minutes; she is unable to correctly copy a rectangle or two intersecting pentagons. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding this patient's driving?

choices.A: The patient should be allowed to drive only with supervision
choices.B: The patient should be allowed to drive short distances only
choices.C: The patient should be allowed to drive until her driving skills are formally assessed
choices.D: The patient should not have access to car keys until her driving skills are formally assessed
choices.E: The patient's driver license should be revoked

correctExplanation: Alzheimer dementia is the most prevalent dementia in elderly patients and is characterized by the loss of intellectual function within multiple domains. It typically presents with progressive cognitive decline that affects a patient's ability to perform instrumental activities of daily living before progressing to affect basic activities of daily living. Examples of instrumental activities of daily living include doing laundry, housework, shopping, preparing meals, taking medications, managing money, and driving. These are more advanced skills and require higher cognitive abilities than do the basic activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, and feeding. In order for elderly adults to remain independent in their homes, they must be able to perform instrumental activities of daily living. A patient's ability to perform activities of daily living can be assessed with a combination of self-reporting, caregiver reporting, and direct observation (eg, driving test, occupational therapy evaluation). In the case of potentially unsafe activities (eg, driving), the unsafe activity should be restricted until formal assessment can happen. Formal assessments can reveal the need for in-home support or a move to an assisted living facility.
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. The patient should be allowed to drive only with supervision (Choice A), the patient should be allowed to drive short distances only (Choice B), and the patient's driver license should be revoked (Choice E) are premature actions. No final decisions about the patient's driving abilities should be made until her abilities are formally assessed. Until this assessment, she should be restricted from driving given that her driving may be unsafe. The patient should be allowed to drive until her driving skills are formally assessed (Choice C) recognizes the need for a formal driving assessment. However, this option introduces danger to the patient and society, as the patient may be an unsafe driver. The patient should be restricted from driving until her driving safety can be assessed.

questionStem: A 4-week-old male infant is brought to the office by his parents because of a 1-week history of 'increasing spit-up.' His parents report that the patient will forcefully spit up within a few minutes after every feeding. He has a history of mild breast-feeding jaundice which resolved spontaneously. The patient was born at term following an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery to a primigravid mother. Vital signs are within normal limits. Palpation over the right upper abdominal quadrant discloses a 1.5-cm mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause of this patient's symptoms?

choices.A: Anteroposterior and decubitus x-rays of the abdomen
choices.C: Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel
choices.E: Observation of the infant while feeding and spitting up

correctExplanation: Pyloric stenosis is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings beginning around age 3 to 6 weeks, such as in this 4-week-old infant. It is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feed, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Repeated vomiting can cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to losses of hydrochloric acid, a major component of gastric secretions. Infants can have severe electrolyte derangements that should be treated urgently. Dehydration can be shown on examination by decreased activity, listlessness, dry mucous membranes, and poor skin turgor. Pyloric stenosis on abdominal examination presents as a small, non-tender mass in the epigastric region. Diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is by ultrasonography of the abdomen showing thickened pyloric musculature. Management includes correcting fluid and electrolyte abnormalities followed by surgical pyloromyotomy.
incorrectExplanation:
Anteroposterior and decubitus x-rays of the abdomen (Choice A) is a nonspecific study that would not necessarily show pyloric stenosis. An x-ray can help with the diagnosis of constipation and bowel obstruction but is neither sensitive nor specific. However, it would not clearly outline hypertrophy of the pylorus. It would not be as helpful as ultrasonography of the abdomen for this patient with pyloric stenosis.

Barium enema with air contrast (Choice B) is used to examine for abnormalities in the large intestine such as colon cancer. It can also be used in children to evaluate for congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) and intestinal malrotation. It is not useful in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis.

Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel (Choice C) can be helpful in the full evaluation of pyloric stenosis and repeated vomiting, which can cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. However, it would only be diagnostic of metabolic derangements and dehydration that can be addressed with supportive measures. Diagnosis and treatment of the underlying cause, pyloric stenosis, should be done using ultrasonography of the abdomen and surgical pyloromyotomy.

questionStem: A 4-week-old boy is brought to the office due to 2 weeks of vomiting. He was born at term via an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and has been exclusively breastfed. It commonly presents with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings beginning around age 3 to 6 weeks, such as in this 4-week-old infant. It is more common in male infants. Repeated bouts of vomiting can cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to losses of hydrochloric acid, a major component of gastric secretions. Infants can have severe electrolyte derangements that should be treated urgently. Dehydration can be shown on examination by decreased activity, listlessness, dry mucous membranes, and poor skin turgor. Pyloric stenosis on abdominal examination presents as a small, nontender mass in the epigastric region. Diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is by ultrasonography of the abdomen showing thickened pyloric musculature. Management includes correcting fluid and electrolyte abnormalities followed by surgical pyloromyotomy.
incorrectExplanation: Anteroposterior and decubitus x-rays of the abdomen (Choice A) is a nonspecific study that would not necessarily show pyloric stenosis. An x-ray can help with the diagnosis of constipation and bowel obstruction but is neither sensitive nor specific. However, it would not clearly outline hypertrophy of the pylorus. It would not be as helpful as ultrasonography of the abdomen for this patient with pyloric stenosis. Barium enema with air contrast (Choice B) is used to examine for abnormalities in the large intestine such as colon cancer. It can also be used in children to evaluate for congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) and intestinal malrotation. It is not useful in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel (Choice C) can be helpful in the full evaluation of pyloric stenosis and repeated vomiting, which can cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. However, it would only be diagnostic of metabolic derangements and dehydration that can be addressed with supportive measures. Diagnosis and treatment of the underlying cause, pyloric stenosis, should be done using ultrasonography of the abdomen and surgical pyloromyotomy. Observation of the infant while feeding and spitting up (Choice E) can be helpful in determining between physiologic regurgitation in infants versus projectile vomiting in pyloric stenosis. However, this patient has a 1.5-cm mass on abdominal palpation, making physiologic regurgitation less likely. Due to palpation of an abdominal mass, further evaluation for pyloric stenosis should be done using ultrasonography of the abdomen.

questionStem: A 24-year-old primigravid woman at 10 weeks’ gestation comes to the office for her first prenatal visit. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Her childhood immunization history is unknown. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. Which of the following is the most appropriate vaccine to administer at this time?
correctExplanation: Routine immunizations indicated during pregnancy include the inactivated influenza virus vaccine and the tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine. The Tdap vaccine is typically administered between weeks 27 and 36 of gestation to optimize maternal antibody response and promote placental transfer of antibodies to the fetus but can be given at any time during the pregnancy. Before infants receive their own diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine at age 2 months, maternal Tdap vaccines protect infants against neonatal tetanus and pertussis, which are associated with significant mortality. To protect infants, patients should receive the Tdap vaccine during each pregnancy (even if the pregnancies occur within the same year). Regardless of gestational age, if a pregnant patient acquires a wound and has not yet received a routine Tdap vaccine during the current pregnancy, standard wound management measures should be adopted (eg, Tdap vaccination in patients with minor wounds who have not received a Tdap vaccine within the past 10 years).
incorrectExplanation: Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E. Hepatitis B (Choice A) vaccine is recommended during pregnancy for patients who have not previously completed the hepatitis B vaccine series. Because this patient’s vaccine history is unknown, titers should be obtained to determine whether she has immunity to hepatitis B. If not, the vaccine should be given. Human papillomavirus (Choice B) vaccine is not typically administered during pregnancy. It has not been studied for its safety of administration during pregnancy. Because of this, it is not a part of the recommended vaccinations administered to pregnant patients. Measles-mumps-rubella (Choice C) and varicella (Choice E) vaccines should not be administered during pregnancy. There is a theoretical risk that a live attenuated vaccine may cause the infant to contract the disease (eg, congenital rubella syndrome). Because of this risk, all live attenuated vaccines should be avoided during pregnancy.

questionStem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of daily expiratory wheezing for 2 weeks. She has also had an occasional cough during exercise and at night. She has had asthma for 2 years treated with inhaled albuterol. Examination shows bilateral expiratory wheezes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Asthma is characterized by reversible obstruction of the bronchi secondary to hyperreactivity and airway inflammation. Patients present with episodes of wheezing, dry cough, and dyspnea. On physical examination, wheezes are heard and there is sometimes a component of prolonged expiration relative to inspiration. Chest x-rays are typically normal. Pulmonary function testing may be normal between symptomatic exacerbations, but during such episodes they show an obstructive pattern with increased residual volume and total lung capacity. The severity of asthma is graded based on frequency of day and nighttime symptomatic episodes. Intermittent asthma is characterized as symptoms occurring less than 2 days per week and less than 2 nights per month and requires as-needed, short-acting bronchodilators for symptomatic relief. Individuals with mild persistent asthma (such as this patient) exhibit symptoms at least 2 days per week or 2 nights per month, which requires the addition of daily inhaled low-dose corticosteroids (eg, fluticasone). Moderate persistent asthma is treated with the addition of inhaled long-acting β2-adrenergic agonists (eg, salmeterol) to the regimen of inhaled low-dose corticosteroids and, as needed, short-acting bronchodilator. Severe persistent asthma is treated with the addition of high-dose corticosteroids to the regimen.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: B, C, D, and E.

Inhaled cromolyn sodium (Choice B) is a therapy that prevents mast-cell degranulation and the release of histamine from mast cells. It can be used in the treatment of asthma and allergic rhinitis. It is not the next step in mild persistent asthma, which is inhaled corticosteroids.

Oral leukotriene inhibitors (Choice C), such as montelukast, are used to prevent smooth muscle contraction and airway edema in asthma. However, they are not as effective as inhaled corticosteroids in the treatment of mild persistent asthma. Thus, this patient with mild persistent asthma should be started on inhaled corticosteroids, which will be more effective in management of her asthma.

Oral prednisone (Choice D) can be used for a short course in acute asthma exacerbations. For long-term pharmacotherapy, oral steroids are only used for patients with severe persistent asthma. This patient has mild persistent asthma, and inhaled steroids are the most appropriate next step.

No additional pharmacotherapy (Choice E) would not be appropriate in this patient with mild persistent asthma. In patients with mild persistent asthma, the addition of inhaled corticosteroids or similar appropriate controller agents is necessary. Patients with intermittent asthma may need no additional pharmacotherapy aside from short-acting bronchodilators, such as albuterol, as needed.

questionStem: A 63-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a 4-day history of a severely itchy rash that started on his right hand and forearm but has since spread to his left hand. This morning, he noticed some "spots" around his waistline. Most of the spots are red bumps, but some of the spots now have turned into scabs. The patient's new roommate, who moved into his apartment a few weeks ago, has had a similar itchy rash. The patient has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of the patient's right hand is shown; similar findings are noted over the waistline. There is no crusting or spreading erythema. He has no rash elsewhere. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy at this time?
correctExplanation: Oral cephalexin is appropriate for treating bacterial skin infections, which is likely given the description of the rash and scabs.

questionStem: A 25-year-old man comes to the office due to a 2-week history of an intensely pruritic rash on his hands. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. The patient recently returned from a camping trip with friends. Physical examination shows excoriations and several small erythematous papules on the fingers and interdigital web spaces. Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
correctExplanation: Scabies is a cutaneous infection caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. Scabies is transmitted from direct skin-to-skin transmission from close contacts. Scabies classically presents with pruritic, superficial burrows and papules of the interweb spaces of the digits, flexural wrist, axillary folds, periumbilical area, waist, and genitalia. Scabies may be diagnosed clinically or following demonstration of mites on skin scrapings of affected areas using mineral oil preparation. Scabies is treated with topical permethrin applied from the neck down on two applications 1 week apart. To prevent recurrence, it is recommended that patients wash all previously worn clothing and bedding in hot water, and dry affected clothing on a hot dryer setting. Additionally, any close contacts of the patient should be treated with permethrin to ensure successful treatment and prevent recurrence. Following treatment, scabies patients may experience pruritus for a few weeks, which is often responsive to oral antihistamines and topical steroids.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Oral acyclovir (Choice A) is the treatment for viral infections, including herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus. Classically, herpes simplex virus presents as a painful cluster of vesicles, which develop into superficial erosions on the skin or mucosal surface. Similarly, herpes zoster, associated with reactivation of varicella zoster virus, is characterized by painful clusters of vesicles distributed in a dermatomal pattern. Acyclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase, thereby preventing viral DNA replication, and is used to treat both herpes simplex and herpes zoster. Acyclovir is not used for the management of scabies infection.

Oral cephalexin (Choice B) is a first-generation cephalosporin that targets gram-positive bacteria. The cephalosporin mechanism of action inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin binding proteins, inhibiting peptidoglycan synthesis of bacterial cell walls. Cephalexin is commonly used to treat skin pathogens including Staphylococcal sp. and Streptococcal sp. While cephalexin may be used to treat bacterial infections, it is not used to treat scabies.

Oral prednisone (Choice C) and topical triamcinolone (Choice E) are glucocorticoids used to treat numerous inflammatory and autoimmune dermatologic conditions. Prednisone may be used for severe flares of inflammatory conditions like eczema or psoriasis; however, abrupt treatment withdrawal is associated with subsequent flaring of these conditions. Prednisone may serve as a bridge to alternative immunomodulatory pharmacologic therapies. Triamcinolone may be used as a midpotency topical steroid to treat numerous inflammatory skin conditions, including eczema and psoriasis. While prednisone and topical triamcinolone may be used for dermatologic conditions, they are not recommended for the acute management of scabies.

questionStem: A previously healthy 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of low back pain that radiates to the left buttock and along the lateral side of the left leg. Her symptoms began 1 day after moving furniture in her home. She has not had fever, chills, constipation, or urinary incontinence. Examination shows diffuse tenderness over the paraspinal muscles of the lumbosacral area and no tenderness over the spine. Range of motion of the left lower extremity is limited by pain. Deep tendon reflexes are normal, muscle strength is intact, and sensory examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: CT scan of the lumbosacral spine

correctExplanation: This patient is likely presenting with acute low back pain secondary to moving furniture in her home. Nonspecific low back pain is a very common occurrence affecting the vast majority of patients seen in primary care. When treating patients with low back pain, it is important to conduct a thorough neurologic examination to evaluate for deficits in sensation or muscle strength as well as changes to deep tendon reflexes. It is common for nonspecific low back pain to present with referred symptoms such as pain radiating into the lower extremities without findings of neurologic deficit. Most patients with acute low back pain, or pain ongoing for less than 4 weeks, will have resolution of their symptoms without further treatment. Additional laboratory studies and imaging are often not necessary in cases of acute low back pain without neurologic deficits identified on examination. Red-flag symptoms which would indicate emergent imaging include new fecal incontinence, urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, or rapidly progressive and significant neurologic deficits. In this case, because of the reassuring physical examination and the patient's 1-week history of symptoms, the most appropriate next step in management would be oral ibuprofen therapy.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Bed rest for 1 week (Choice A) is not an appropriate treatment for acute low back pain. Patients who undergo bed rest have been shown to experience increasingly severe pain and have a slower recovery. In this case, oral ibuprofen therapy is the most appropriate next step in management.

CT scan of the lumbosacral spine (Choice B) may be a reasonable next step in management if red-flag symptoms such as new fecal incontinence, urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, or rapidly progressive and significant neurologic deficits were present on exam. Typically, MRI is the preferred emergent imaging modality, but CT scan can be used if there are contraindications to MRI. This patient does not have neurologic deficits identified on examination, making ibuprofen the most appropriate next step in management.

Epidural corticosteroid injection (Choice C) may be a reasonable treatment option for patients presenting with radiculopathy. Lumbar radiculopathy often presents as pain radiating from the lumbar spine into the lower extremities with the presence of motor or sensory deficits or changes in deep tendon reflexes. This patient is presenting with referred pain into the lower extremities without neurologic changes, making ibuprofen the most appropriate next step in management.

questionStem: A 55-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-week history of a recurrent and severely itchy diffuse rash. The patient reports that the rash typically resolves within 3 to 4 hours and is most severe over his back. He has not had fever, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, or any other symptoms. Use of diphenhydramine during the episodes provides moderate relief. He has no history of serious illness and takes no routine medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. The patient does not currently have a rash but shows a previously taken photograph of his back. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study at this time?

choices.B: Complete blood count with leukocyte differential

correctExplanation: C1-esterase inhibitor testing is appropriate for diagnosing hereditary angioedema, which can present with recurrent episodes of swelling and rash.

questionStem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the office due to a 2-day history of a rash. She has no significant medical history and takes no medications. The patient does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 14/min. Physical examination shows multiple, raised, erythematous lesions on the trunk and arms. The lesions are intensely pruritic and blanch with pressure. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Complete blood count with leukocyte differential
choices.E: No further diagnostic studies are indicated

correctExplanation: Urticaria or hives are characterized by transient skin or mucosal swelling associated with pink, pruritic wheals. Clinically, individual urticarial lesions resolve within 24 hours. Urticaria develops from mast-cell degranulation and subsequent release of vasoactive substances, including histamine, into the surrounding skin. There are multiple triggers of mast-cell degranulation, including allergens presented by IgE antibodies, substance P, C5a, and medications. Most cases of urticaria are idiopathic, although urticaria may be associated with upper respiratory tract infections, drugs including aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs), and certain foods. While hives are self-limited, symptomatic treatments include oral antihistamines, epinephrine in cases associated with anaphylaxis, and omalizumab, a monoclonal antibody that binds IgE, in cases of chronic, refractory urticaria. No additional workup is required in the management of acute urticaria in the absence of other symptoms or presenting features.
incorrectExplanation: A, B, C, and D. C1-esterase inhibitor testing (Choice A) is used in the workup of hereditary or acquired angioedema. Angioedema is characterized by swellings in the dermis and subcutaneous or submucosal tissue. Angioedema commonly affects the larynx, lips, eyelids, genital region, and/or abdominal wall. Unlike in urticaria, cases of angioedema may last for 2 to 3 days. Triggers for angioedema include food allergies, insect stings, and medications including aspirin, NSAIDs, and iodinated contrast. While C1-esterase inhibitor testing is warranted in angioedema, this patient's clinical presentation is consistent with urticaria. Complete blood count with leukocyte differential (Choice B) may be utilized in patients with refractory urticaria when there is concern for a lymphoproliferative disorder or hypereosinophilic syndrome. Hypereosinophilic syndrome can be associated with the development of eczema, hives, or angioedema, in addition to end-organ dysfunction. Hypereosinophilic syndrome has been associated with F1P1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene, leading to a constitutive activated tyrosine kinase. This patient's presentation is not consistent with hypereosinophilic syndrome. Radioallergosorbent testing (Choice C) is a blood test used to detect specific IgE antibodies. Development of IgE antibodies is associated with type I (immediate) hypersensitivity syndromes, which may trigger hives or anaphylaxis. Radioallergosorbent testing may be used to detect food allergies, pet dander allergies, and other environmental allergies. While radioallergosorbent testing may be used to test for potential allergens, it is not recommended in the workup of uncomplicated, acute urticaria. Serum C3 and C4 concentrations (Choice D) may be tested in the workup of angioedema. Most cases of hereditary and acquired angioedema are associated with a decreased concentration of C4. Normal C4 concentration may be associated with idiopathic angioedema, angioedema associated with hypereosinophilia, and ACE-inhibitor associated angioedema. While C4 concentrations may be tested in the workup of angioedema, it is not recommended in the initial workup of urticaria.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. One year ago, her serum cholesterol concentration was 260 mg/dL, and she was started on a low-fat diet. She has no history of serious illness. Her Pap smears during the past 10 years have shown no abnormalities. Her last Pap smear was 1 year ago. Her mother has type 2 diabetes mellitus, and her father died of colon cancer at the age of 62 years. The patient does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She has been married for 15 years. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 77 kg (170 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m². Her pulse is 64/min, and blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Increased serum concentrations of lipids, including low-density cholesterol, are associated with an increased risk for coronary vascular disease. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has recommended screening for hyperlipidemia in all men greater than age 35 years and in all women greater than age 45 years who are at an increased risk for coronary vascular disease. They also recommend initiating a statin medication in such persons age 40 to 75 years who are at an increased 10-year risk (greater than 10%) of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Other risk factors for coronary vascular disease include hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, a positive family history of coronary vascular disease, and smoking. Optimization of serum lipids with pharmacologic treatment and lifestyle modification can reduce the risk for coronary vascular disease and myocardial infarction. Statins remain the first-line pharmacologic therapy for most patients with hyperlipidemia. This patient should have her serum cholesterol concentration rechecked after implementing her lifestyle modifications 1 year ago, and if it is still increased, further interventions should be initiated.
incorrectExplanation:
Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, and E.

Colonoscopy (Choice A) is not currently indicated because of the patient’s age. The USPSTF recommends routine colorectal cancer screening for all patients beginning at age 45 years and continuing until age 75 years. Patients with a family history of colon cancer should have their first colonoscopy screening at age 40 years or 10 years younger than the age their family member was at the time of diagnosis.

5-Hour glucose tolerance test (Choice B) may be a useful test for the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, though it has been replaced by alternative screening methods and shorter protocol times of glucose tolerance. The USPSTF recommends screening for abnormal blood glucose or diabetes mellitus in patients age 35 to 70 years who are overweight or diagnosed with obesity. Currently, fasting blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c are the preferred screening tests.

Mammography (Choice C) is not indicated at this time. The USPSTF recommends screening mammography every 2 years for women age 50 to 74 years. Women with a family history of breast cancer may begin screening earlier.

Pap smear (Choice E) is not indicated at this time. The USPSTF recommends cervical cancer screening with Pap smear every 3 years for women age 21 to 65 years. Women age 30 to 65 years may also be screened with a combination of Pap smear and human papillomavirus (HPV) testing every 5 years.
